speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance, whom I am sure we all welcome back to the house on his return from the United Kingdom. My question deals precisely with his trip to the United Kingdom where he had talks concerning trade problems. I wonder whether the minister would give the house a report on those talks, and particularly will he explain the technical difficulties which he said beset trade between the two countries, to which he referred in one of his talks, and which has been described as "cold comfort" by some of the British authorities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON TRIP TO U.K. BY FINANCE MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for his kindly words, although I do not know about the references to cold comfort. The British government through its officials did complain some time ago about the application of our anti-dumping procedures and, I think it was last February, the Minister of Trade and Commerce undertook that we would make a study of their complaints. This we have done.

Inquiries of the Ministry
When I was in London I reported to various ministers of Her Majesty's government there and also to a number of industrialists, and during a course of a speech I made a statement. I said that we have concluded that these obstacles, or alleged obstacles, did not in themselves, in our view, constitute a major difficulty but that there were some justifiable grounds for complaints and we intended to do something about these.
I pointed that this would require legislation. I also pointed out that we were very anxious that in the process of correcting the difficulties in question we did not do something which would create new ones, and that this would take some time to work out. I said also that Canada had complaints about certain non-tariff barriers to trade as applied to us by certain other countries, and that we hoped this whole matter could be dealt with in the context of the negotiations leading to the Kennedy round.

In participating in this debate in a week which has seen the 97 th anniversary of confederation, an anniversary marking the beginning of our history as a nation, one cannot fail to be conscious of the fact that those who now speak are taking part in an event which in future years may well be looked upon as among the more significant in this history. This government's proposal to parliament for a national flag for Canada is but one part of the evolutionary process that began with confederation and continued with the imperial conference of 1926 and the statute of Westminster in 1931. In fact it might be said that this proposal is basically a reflection of the status that has been ours completely, at least since 1931, a status which many today feel should now be clearly evidenced by the symbols we use to identify our nationhood.
As a younger member of this house, Mr. Speaker, I consider that the opportunity to participate in these debates is perhaps one of the greatest honours and privileges that can come to any Canadian. I am deeply conscious of the responsibilities that must fall upon 20220-3174
Canadian Flag
everyone who is given this opportunity. One of these responsibilities is the duty to make decisions on matters of national importance, a duty which none of us have any real right to cast aside or shirk because we find there are strong differences of public opinion on the question. It is true that members must give very serious consideration to the views of all those who may call upon them as their representatives to oppose this proposal. However, members must also consider no less seriously the views of those who call upon them, also as their representatives, to support it. Being asked to make decisions on matters of national importance upon which there is not already any complete agreement amongst the people is the very essence of our parliamentary system. This system, to paraphrase the words of Edmund Burke, demands of members elected by the people that they bring to parliament not only their industry, not only their efforts on behalf of their constituents, but also their judgment which they must be prepared to exercise in the national interest.
If we are not really willing to take our responsibility to make a decision as members of parliament and as a parliament on this question, how can we refuse those who may insist on a referendum on the Canada pension plan or a national health plan? These are also issues of great national importance that touch the lives of all persons in Canada in a direct way that even something as important as a national flag can never do. Those favouring the referendum have not given any compelling reason as yet, and I do not believe they can, as to why this procedure should be suitable and, in fact, is needed for this flag proposal and at the same time should not be used for other matters of national concern.
Those opposing this government's flag proposal have spoken often of tradition, of its importance, of its value for our present day existence. They say, quite wrongly I think, that in making this proposal our traditions, our heritage, particularly those parts coming from Britain, are being cast aside. Yet at the same time, by moving this amendment calling for a referendum they are urging in fact that we cast aside the concept that lies at the very core of our British political traditions. I refer to the basic concept that members of parliament, once elected by the people, have a duty to make decisions on matters upon which there is no unanimity of public opinion. The official opposition is, in fact, asking us to cast aside that part of our British tradition that says the making of decisions on matters of public

Canadian Flag
importance by referendum is not a part of our political institutions, political institutions which have evolved over the centuries, first in Britain and later here in our own country. In rejecting this tradition they would follow one that is still essentially foreign to us, that of the republican system in the United States, in some parts of which the referendum is an accepted part of the process of government.
I was very impressed with the words spoken over 20 years ago by the present Leader of the Opposition when he opposed the plebiscite in 1942 and asked that the parliament of Canada be allowed to decide the issue. Surely those words are no less applicable today.
It has been suggested also that a referendum or plebiscite on the flag issue would enhance national unity. The experience of this country with the plebiscite of 1942 would indicate that it would do exactly the opposite, emphasizing possible divisions between sectors of our country and in fact creating them where they might not have existed before.
The tradition of our parliamentary system against deciding issues by referendum is reflected and followed by the approach taken by various national organizations. I, and I think most people in this house and in the country, have been very impressed by the wonderful work of the Canadian Legion for physical fitness and in looking after the interests of veterans of all our wars. But I have also been impressed by the fact that the Legion did not take a referendum amongst all its members before substituting the maple leaf for the union jack on its own badge. Instead, this decision was made by the elected delegates of the membership in convention assembled, even though many individual legionnaires, I understand, were strongly opposed to this move. Nor was a referendum of all its members taken to see whether they approved its current official stand on the red ensign. Instead this policy, which I respect, was again adopted by a vote of the delegates assembled in convention, and again even though it is apparent that not all its members support this stand.
I say this since men like Colonel Keiller MacKay, a co-founder of the Legion, support the proposed maple leaf flag. In so far as I am aware, none of the organizations that are urging the adoption of the red ensign or a national referendum on the flag issue have themselves held a referendum among their members to gain prior approval of their position.
Tradition has often been referred to in this debate. Various opposition members have

wrongly suggested that in adopting the maple leaf flag we will be adopting a flag bearing a symbol without any tradition. The maple leaf is also a central part of our Canadian tradition. The speeches of the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Leeds among others, illustrate this very well. If it is important to have our traditions reflected in our flag, then let us choose a symbol which is part of this tradition but which will enable us to have a flag which cannot be mistaken for that of any other country. Perhaps most important of all, it should be a symbol which all Canadians, no matter what their origin may be, can hold equally as their own.
The three maple leaves conjoined on a single stem, I suggest to this house, is in fact such a symbol. The maple leaf is rooted deep in Canadian tradition. It has been used by the people living on this northerly half of the North American continent to distinguish themselves from others in the human spectrum, to identify themselves as something different-as "Canadians"-since the visit of the Prince of Wales in 1860, eight years before confederation.
The maple leaf has been the symbol that Canadians have been using to identify themselves to friend and foe alike in the battles in two world wars and since then in the peace keeping operations of the United Nations in the far corners of the world. There is no other symbol that is as readily understood as saying "I stand for Canada", by people both within our country and around the world as clearly and as unmistakably as the maple leaf.
Traditions of Britain, especially those involving our political institutions, traditions of France and of other countries as well, all form part of our heritage and therefore of our own traditions, but they form part of our heritage as Canadians. They have all been shaped and altered by the buffeting winds of Canadian conditions and events. The three maple leaves on one stem are clearly a key part of our tradition, and a national flag for Canada based on this symbol will reflect this tradition and therefore all our heritage, but it will do so in a way that is distinctively Canadian.
I know there are those who are troubled over the prospect of a Canadian flag which does not bear in some part the union jack. I respect these views and the sincerity with which they are held, but let it not be forgotten that this government has also proposed that parliament declare that the union

jack may be flown as a symbol of Canada's links with crown and commonwealth.
I feel that approval by parliament of a national flag based on an emblem which all Canadians can hold equally as their own, no matter what their origin or ancestry, will be a major step toward creating a greater degree of national unity. It will be a major step toward creating a spirit of positive Canadianism that up until now has not been sufficiently developed in all aspects of our national life; a spirit of Canadianism such that a citizen of our country, whether he speaks English or French or both these languages, will consider himself first and foremost a Canadian and will also be considered as such by all his fellow citizens no matter what his ancestry might be.
I am proud to be able to participate in an event which may stand out in our national history. I know that in doing so it is not my wish, or the wish of those on this side of the house who support this proposal, to destroy or take anything away. Instead, we want to raise higher on the foundations of the past, the already imposing structure of Canadian nationhood, and take a step which I am convinced will soon result in a stronger and more united Canada. We are the inheritors and guardians of our country's past but we cannot be its captives, for we have equally important responsibilities to build our country's present and its future.
I am told that the grave of each Canadian who fell in battle in two world wars is marked with the maple leaf. We, the living, have given them this symbol so the world would know the country and ideals for which they died. Mr. Speaker, we the living, for ourselves and for those who will come after, can do no less than to adopt this same symbol and these ideals for this country today and for the ages.

Mr. Speaker, I have noticed that several hon. members who spoke in this debate during the past few hours, including the last speaker, have quoted Edmund Burke. I too intend to quote him and to point out that in 1769 he said:
There is, however, a limit at which forebearance ceases to be a virtue.
I use that as an introduction to what I have to say, not because I wish to take part in this debate from any rancour or bitterness, nor is it my intention to cause offence to any member of this house or to any group in Canada regardless of the views they hold. Although I may not agree with their views I
Canadian Flag
will defend their rights to express them. I ask only for myself and for the people for whom I speak that same right, not only in this debate but in the flag under which we are expected to live.
I believe in all sincerity that this statement of Edmund Burke has application to the present situation. I believe in all sincerity this point has now been reached in Canada. I believe that we English speaking Canadians-and I do not speak for all English speaking Canadians, but in this regard I speak for a very large number of them- have been guilty of a disservice to our country and we have been unfair to our French speaking Canadian compatriots because we have been too silent for too long. We have been too long suffering in the face of attacks on many of the things that most of us hold dear, and I have come to believe that we have remained silent in an attempt to prevent giving offence to our fellow countrymen of French extraction.
We have followed this course because we refused to believe that the great majority of French speaking Canadians are truly represented by the loud and often hysterical voices of extremists. However, the voices of moderation and reasonableness in French Canada have been largely ignored, at least in the news media of English speaking Canada. It is the Rene Levesques and the other extremists who are the delight of the C.B.C. and of those in the newspaper business whose stock in trade it is to sell newspapers with headlines screaming of intolerance.
By our silence we have implied approval of extremists who would divide us, and we have discouraged those of temperate attitude who would unite the country. On this question there are many people from all parts of Canada and many voices from Quebec- though largely ignored so far as news media are concerned-who recognize the reasonable rights of English speaking Canadians. They realize that English speaking Canadians have symbols that they hold dear, but these voices have been largely submerged by other more extreme views, leaving the impression in English speaking Canada that nothing brings satisfaction to French speaking Canada except that which will cause pain and anxiety to English speaking Canada.
This is a most unfortunate situation, and I for one do not believe for one moment that this is the true voice of French speaking Canada. It has been made to appear that the demand of French Canada is not to have in our flag a greater representation of the things

Canadian Flag
it holds dear, but the impression has been created that French speaking Canadians want one thing and one thing only, the removal of the union jack and other symbols, whether of French or British origin, from our flag.
That has caused a polarization, a reaction as natural as day following night. When that has been put forward as the official attitude of French speaking Canadians there has naturally been a reaction and the unfortunate thing is that there is polarization of opinion around the proposal of the government on the one hand, because it excludes the union jack from our national flag, and on the other hand there has been a rallying around the red ensign because it is something around which to rally and is the status quo. I think the wrong approach has been taken in the handling of this whole matter.
I support this amendment, of course. I rise to support the amendment to the resolution, not because it is the ideal thing but because it would be an improvement on the proposal of the government if the house would accept it.
I consider that I have a duty to put on the record and bring to the attention of the government not only my own views on this matter but also the views of the vast majority of the people I represent, because I am informed that these are views of large numbers of my constituents. In my constituency at the present time the people are occupied with celebrating the 100th anniversary of the first meeting of the fathers of confederation in Charlottetown, which led up to confederation.
Hear, hear.

I am proud to represent the constituency in which that first meeting took place. The people of my constituency are, at the same time, worried that there is evidence of tendencies which will not assist national unity at a time when we are reaching the 100th anniversary of a very important date. Large numbers of my constituents-almost all of them-feel strongly that the union jack should be retained in any Canadian national flag. Most of them would support the red ensign. Most of them would agree with Mackenzie King's point of view which is expressed in an article which I read just recently written by Mr. James McCook and appearing in the Ottawa Journal, Mr. McCook says:
Just alter the last war this reporter went through Belgium and Holland with Mr. King and in the evenings, after the honours of the day had been done him at meetings large and small,

he used to tell us that if Canadians could see the respect given the red ensign in Europe they would have no doubt about what their flag should be.
Most of the deep trouble we are now in as a nation over this very important and potentially divisive problem is due to political deception and deceit. No party in this house is free from guilt in this connection. I am one who believes that you can never arrive at honest and correct conclusions if you do not at least attempt to start with valid premises. As I said, no party is free from political deceit in this matter, and it is a sad commentary on this state of affairs that at the present time the strength of the various parties in this house is roughly in direct proportion to their guilt in this matter.
I hope this is only coincidental. Both major parties bear more responsibility in this connection than do the others, because they are national parties and seek support in all parts of Canada. Both major parties have passed resolutions within their ranks supporting a distinctive flag, and I sincerely believe that the only reason these resolutions could have passed at the annual meetings of either of the major parties is that the word "distinctive" is deceitful in itself, because it means different things to different people, depending on what part of the country they come from.
Hear, hear.

In English speaking Canada we believe that we now have a distinctive flag. The order in council that established it says so. The prime minister of the day, Mr. Mackenzie King, believed so. The order in council says in part:
-and that it shall be appropriate to fly the Canadian red ensign within or without Canada wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
That is one end of the spectrum of the various interpretations of the word "distinctive". At the other end of the spectrum is the view that a distinctive Canadian flag means anything as long as it has not on it the union jack or any other symbols of European countries from which we derive our origins, regardless of what groups may be involved.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

When I am finished. I do not propose to allow myself to be interrupted at this time. The Prime Minister has said that he insists upon parliament dealing with this matter at this time because he

was given a mandate by the Canadian people in the last election campaign; because the establishment of a distinctive flag within two years of assuming office was one of the planks of their platform.
Nothing could be more unreal than that contention. I am certain that in many parts of Canada the people voted for the present government in spite of that item in their platform and not on account of it. Never on any occasion, to my knowledge, did the Prime Minister stand up and say what he meant by a distinctive Canadian flag. I am as certain as I am that I am standing here that there are constituencies in Canada that would have taken a very strong line had the Prime Minister done this. If he had stood up in public with the design which the government proposes and said "If I become prime minister this will be the flag, and there will be no reference to the union jack or other symbols on it", I am sure that many of his supporters now in the House of Commons would not have been elected.
Hear, hear.

In other parts of Canada, if the Liberal candidates had stood up and proclaimed this they would not even have been nominated by their party. In addition to this, the flag issue was a minor issue in that campaign; it was interwoven with many other isues. The government does not know whether it was elected partly on account of the flag or partly in spite of it. In point of fact, only 42 per cent of the Canadian people saw fit to vote for this government, and the majority of our people decided not to do so.
Has the government a mandate? No. If proof is required I could refer to letters I have received from people in my constituency who have been traditionally Liberal and all their lives have supported the Liberal party. Their views on this matter would convince any reasonable man that the government has not a mandate in this connection. I should like to quote briefly from one letter. The reference is to the Prime Minister:
An election now, with feelings hot about the flag, would see many diehard Liberals voting away from his party.
That is referring to the Prime Minister. The letter continues:
He undoubtedly will be replaced and put out to pasture. Goodness knows, he has done enough harm already.
That is the reaction that this flag question has stirred up in my riding. In addition, Mr. Speaker, can it be contended, for example,
Canadian Flag
that the premier of Newfoundland worked hard to bring this government to power because it was going to eliminate the union jack and other symbols from our national flag? Of course not. Mr. Speaker, back on May 15-I remember the date because it happens to be my birthday-the Prime Minister gave this house a great, long list of important legislation which we should deal with before a summer recess. There was no mention of the flag debate at that time. On May 12, prior to that, when there was still no indication when the flag issue would come up, the Prime Minister said that members of the house would be allowed to vote according to their conscience. The following week, on May 19, it was a question of confidence in the government, and he indicated that an unfavourable vote would bring on an election. On May 26 he said that the resolution would be on the order paper the next day, I believe it was.
Now, what happened in the interval to change this attitude? The only thing that happened of which we know was that the Prime Minister went to Winnipeg and addressed the Canadian Legion. I do not know what he expected the result of that address would be. I would draw no conclusions, but it does remind me of something which happened on December 29, 1170 when another petulant person in power said, because he was miffed, "Will nobody rid me of this insolent priest?" So four retainers galloped off to Canterbury and murdered Thomas a Becket.
The situation here could be explained by somebody saying: "Will nobody rid me of these insolent Royal Canadian Legionnaires?" So somebody came up with this resolution, to stuff it down the throats of Canadians who stand for all they believe in and what they wish to have in their flag without trying to exclude the things anybody else believes in.
Even if the government had a mandate and a majority-and it has neither-to pass far reaching legislation, this is no ordinary legislation. A flag should be as permanent as a country itself. No parliament can bind future parliaments, so that if this parliament by a simple majority can decree what is to be our national flag, each future parliament in turn can replace that flag with one of its choice. What a dismal precedent; what a dismal and divisive prospect this holds out for us.
Democratic government as we understand it presupposes an understanding by those

Canadian Flag
in power of the rights of minorities. The notion that a ruler has the moral right to do anything that he has the technical power to do is the philosophy of a despot. A flag should have in it symbols which will lift the pride and inspire the patriotism of all groups who live under it, especially those who feel strongly about the symbols they hold dear. It should be a unifying force, not a divisive one. This is no age for anyone to issue a sort of ukase, forcing down the throats of the Canadian people the personal choice of any man or small group of men. Such action will split this country from sea to sea, not unite it. It is not important to me whether the split is down the middle, to one side or to the other; it is the split itself which Canada cannot stand at this time.
There are many Canadians in French speaking Canada as well as in English speaking Canada who recognize that the most important thing Canada needs at this time is unity, and there should be a unifying force in the symbols under which we live. Excellent suggestions have been made that it should be a matter of compromise. For example, there is the very attractive approach to this question of the flag suggested by Mr. Jean Dubuc, 730 Talus, Ste Foy, Quebec; another from Paul E. Marcoux, 9054 St. Hubert street, Montreal 11, Quebec, and another from Mr. J. D. Davidson, of Debert, Nova Scotia, all of them recognizing that there is a need for symbols in a flag which will represent the various groups that make up this Canada of ours and give each group a reason to have pride when that flag is flying.
It is my sincere belief that minority groups have rights in this matter, but this is not to say that minorities alone have rights and that the majority has none. I believe that minority groups have a right to have the symbols they love and cherish represented in our flag. But just as emphatically I believe that no group has the right to dictate to any other group what that group cannot have in its flag. I think this applies whether the groups concerned are majorities or minorities.
I am a member of a very large group of Canadians who passionately believe that the symbols of our origin should be retained in any flag chosen to fly over us. France has given us much; but I am a Canadian of other than French extraction so I do not believe it is my right even to suggest to French speaking Canadians what they should have to represent them in their flag, much less to 
suggest what they cannot have to represent them in their flag. I am speaking, of course, of the national flag.
I will, however, speak for the people I do represent. These people come from many racial groups-Scottish, English, Irish. There are also many Acadian French. Then there are lesser numbers of Germans, Dutch, Danes, and even smaller numbers from other nationalities, including Chinese, Lebanese, etc., plus a few native Indians. No priority is attached to the list except in terms of numbers. With the exception of the last named all these people, or if not they their ancestors, as the case applies, came to live under the union jack out of choice. If I am asked whether I include the Acadian French, I do; because at the capitulation at the fortress of Louisburg when Prince Edward Island was covered, the terms of the capitulation provided were that French settlers in Prince Edward Island should have the right to be repatriated to France in ships sailing under cartel free from molestation by either of the combating sides.
The ancestors of the Acadians I represent chose to stay and live under British rule. They made great contributions in all fields, in the professions and in government. For example, at the present time the mayor of Charlottetown is of Acadian extraction, as is also the minister of welfare and labour, to cite only two. The flag which these people have chosen to live under is known all over the world as the flag of freedom. Everywhere the union jack is flown it has left legacies of values which we all cherish regardless of our racial background; freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom of the press and freedom to elect a legislature in a fully democratic way.
Now, it is fair to ask: If the government has taken the wrong approach to this matter, what is the right approach? My belief is that the right approach is to assess in some democratic way the wishes of the various groups in Canada as to what symbols they want to have to represent them in their national flag. This could have been done by members of parliament had they been given the right to freely express the opinions of their constituents in a free vote. Or it could have been done by a committee composed of members of all parties represented in this house. But the door has been closed on that. There is, of course, the possibility of a plebiscite such as this amendment proposes, and there are other ways. One would be a federal-provincial conference at which the provincial

governments could assist the federal parliament by expressing the views of the people they govern as to what they would like to see in a flag.
I do not maintain that the provinces would have the right to select a national flag. I suggest such a meeting only as a source of valid information. The Prime Minister says why call on the provinces? The provinces have developed provincial flags of their own without reference to the federal government. That is true, but I am sure the provinces in selecting those flags ascertained the wishes of the people in the various parts of those provinces and had those wishes reflected in the flags which were chosen.
Another way of proceeding would be to call a national conference on this matter, at which various organizations would have the right to make representations as a means of channeling up to the government the real wishes of the country in regard to this matter. After all, a flag is a thing of the heart. There are millions of Canadians who want the union jack retained in the flag in some way. At the present time many of them who would not otherwise do so support the red ensign simply as a reaction to the demand of the government that the union jack be removed from the flag. But these are reasonable people. They would be willing to compromise. It is true they want the union jack, but many of them would not care if it were in lengthwise or sideways or even edgewise, as long as it was there. They put great stock upon the union jack. They know it to be a flag of freedom, a flag of Christendom. They feel that any move, especially by a minority government, to deprive them of it would be an infringement of their rights even though the government estimated it had the power to do so.
Prime ministers come and go, but the flag should be a permanent thing. Only last Saturday one of my constituents in conversation with me summed up the attitude of many of my constituents by saying "We are approaching a deadlock on this matter, but there is a a perfectly simple solution. Leave the flag alone and change the Prime Minister."
Hear, hear.

Then, when the wishes of the various groups in this country as to the symbols they hold dear have been appraised and measured, a committee of all parties in the house, including representatives from the Senate, could work on a design for a flag incorporating those symbols. Such a committee should have with it to assist it a 20220-318
Canadian Flag
group of advisers, a panel of heraldic experts. One such who comes to my mind is Dr. Conrad Swan, a Canadian who has achieved preeminence in this field. I suggest the assistance of this panel of experts because the final design of a national flag is a very intricate thing, not simply as a pennant but because of the many and various uses to which it has to be put. A flag should be suitable for all these variations.
We are now considering a resolution which would proclaim this particular pattern as the national flag. There is no indication what result this would have on not only the Canadian red ensign but on the Canadian blue ensign which is flown by all government ships. There is no indication what will become of the air force flag of Canada, a beautiful flag which has come to be loved especially by those who have served in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and almost a quarter of a million people served in that force during the second world war alone.
That is repetition.
That may be true, but I have a right to repeat this on behalf of the constituents I represent.
Hear, hear.

I have no objection to the maple leaf as a symbol to be included in a Canadian flag. It has been used as a trademark of Canada, usually in conjunction with some other symbols, for many years. But to me a maple leaf by itself is not adequate for a flag, whether there be three leaves or one.
What do you want?

I will tell the hon. member; just give me time. I believe a flag should not be a pictorial representation of the flora or fauna of any particular geographic region. It should stand for something much more significant than that. I have no objection to the maple leaf being used in addition to the symbols we hold dear. The three crosses in the union jack represent, for example, England, Scotland and Ireland. They also represent the Christian heritage which we all pretend, at least, to support. The union jack was arrived at by a reasonable process of compromise. Had the flag of either Scotland or England been imposed on the other, there would not have been such a relatively easy blending of two nations which were at each other's throats for centuries.

What about Ireland?

Canadian Flag

We of Anglo-Saxon,
Scottish and Irish origin put great stock in this because these crosses go back to the days of the crusades, the time when the west was threatened by a growing wave of Mohammedanism. At the time of the French revolution France discarded Christian symbols from its flag, but in the dark days of 1940, 1941 and 1942, when France had been overrun and was represented only by the free French expatriots, they returned to a Christian symbol in the form of the cross of Lorraine.
That was not the flag of the French, and you know it.
The hon. member will have many opportunities to take part in this debate and correct any errors he believes I have made.
I am correcting one now.

I must say that now, when our way of life is threatened and our very civilization is in jeopardy from those who would engulf us, to see the symbols of Christendom struck from our masthead would give those forces nothing but cheer.
I am astonished at so many of those who look on themselves as champions of Christendom but who are dupes in such a process. Those who would submerge us in this world struggle for men's minds know full well that a rootless people cannot survive. Edmund Burke again has said that people will not look forward to posterity who never look backward to their ancestors. The way of subversion is to bring into disrepute by any means the system of government; respect for law and order; to erode the values by which we live; destroy the symbols of our history, weaken our resolve to defend the principles for which we stand. Once these things are accomplished the rest of the course is easy for those who would subvert us.
Unfortunately there has been let loose in this land in recent times a trend to intolerance which gives ready will to use the opposite race as a scapegoat for all the ills that any single group feels are theirs. It is so simple to blame it on the English or blame it on the French when in actual fact this is not the cause of the trouble at all.
The intemperate demands of one segment against the whole, this vicious, ever-accelerating frenzy in which the maximum demands of yesterday become the minimum demands of today, can lead nowhere but to destruction. The ignorance of our history in some parts of Canada is pathetic, and I am not

speaking of any particular racial group now. I saw recently that among high school graduates there were only 10 per cent, I believe, who knew who was the first prime minister of Canada, and they did not know who any of the others were.
What disturbs me is that we have these unfavourable trends which are becoming accentuated and which will divide our country. I say sincerely and without recrimination that as far as I can see the government's approach to this problem is to feed this crocodile well in the hope that it will eat them last.

Mr. Speaker, I believe sincerely, like millions of other English speaking Canadians, that our compatriots in French Canada are not represented truly-
