I understood I had agreement, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I proceeded. I am nearly finished. I want to make one personal observation at this point. I wish to say that I have the highest regard for French speaking Canadians. I have associated with them closely. I have lived with them for years. For two years I had the honour to command a little R.A.F. unit overseas which was made up of officers from New Zealand, Australia and Canada. I was proud that the Canadian representation in that unit were all French Canadians except myself. We worked together with the greatest and closest harmony. There has been no loss of the mutual regard we had for each other, with the result that even to this day we exchange our children in the summertime so that our children will have the opportunity to learn something of the opposite language and to see that people of the opposite race in Canada do not have horns.
I know the Prime Minister is not present at the moment but the Secretary of State is here, and there is something I should like to say. I say it in no sense, believe me, of any party taking political advantage of anyone. But I plead with the Prime Minister at this time to reconsider, to back away from this course of action, because I am sure it will

have a divisive effect on Canada and cause wounds that will not be healed for many years.
That is what you are doing now.

That is not what I am doing now. My proposal is that all racial groups in Canada, especially the two founding races, have symbols in our flag of which we can each be proud. I contend that neither race has the right to say what the other cannot have on the flag. In effect that is what is being said to us at the present time, and we resent it. I should like at this point to substantiate what I have said by reading a brief letter addressed to me. It reads as follows:
W/C. The Hon. J. A. MacLean, D.F.C.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
There has been a great deal of controversy recently concerning the proposed distinctive national flag and our association feels that we should make known to you our preferences in this regard. The united services officers club of Charlottetown includes in its membership nearly all of the officers of the armed forces resident in Prince Edward Island-
I might interject that it includes all retired officers as well as presently serving officers.
-and it seems to us that, as leaders of Canada's military forces in war and peace our opinion should be of assistance to you in resolving this difficult problem.
A special general meeting of all members of the club was held the evening of May 29 in the club rooms and the following motion was passed: That we are opposed to any Canadian flag which does not incorporate the union jack.
May we respectively solicit your support in this respect?
Yours truly,
Ian G. Kerry President of U.S.O.C.
May I say that this is not some minor club. It has among its membership nearly all the leading citizens of Prince Edward Island by virtue of the fact that they have held commissions in the services at one time or another. I ask the Prime Minister to put patriotism ahead of party, or whatever the motivation is in this case. Give time for consideration. This is a great issue. It is not fair to parliament or to the Canadian people to expect it to be resolved in a headlong rush at a time when we are all under tensions and frustrations and when another look at this matter would be of great advantage.
Canadian Flag
The Prime Minister should realize that Canada is not a monolith that has to conform to the specifications of any one man or any one group. Canada is a mosaic contributed to by all the various groups. Only the day before yesterday this was so well depicted by the very fine program on the front lawn initiated by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I congratulate him on it. There you had a representation of the contribution of all the ethnic groups and the various cultures that go to make Canada into one worth while mosaic.
I will not go into it now, but I would refer the Secretary of State to the fact that problems of this very type arose in South Africa in the 1920's. The government of the day there started out with exactly the same technique, but they had the good sense to retreat from it and not to divide the house on the matter on second reading of their legislation. Eventually committees were established and a compromise was reached in which all parties and all the people represented in that parliament could at least acquiesce.
This is the only way, Mr. Speaker, that we can work toward unity in this country. If you want evidence in support of that fact I would say that in spite of the difficulties experienced by the whites in South Africa, who were so disturbed about this matter in the twenties, they are now more united than they have ever been before. I say that if the Prime Minister is a man, and I believe he is, he will not divide the country on this issue. If he is a statesman, I believe that he will not even divide this parliament on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, in rising in this debate on the amendment moved by the Conservatives to have the matter of the flag settled through a referendum, I must admit that one thing amazed me. While I listened to certain Canadians, certain English speaking representatives, one after the other-especially those from the Conservative group, although there were some from the New Democratic party and even from the Thompsonists-I noted that members of that little group which is somewhat like the Tory spirit brooding over parliament to sow discord, in a quite desperate effort, wept their last tears in an incoherent language, always the same, mourning the loss of the red ensign.

Canadian Flag
Mr. Speaker, do you honestly think a man could lose what he never had? Is it even possible to regret what you have never owned?
Indeed, in 1945, our troops could never be told from British troops. Other countries could not single out our troops who were always at the line of Are in all British wars. Canada having no identification flag, her government decided, in September 1945, since they could not succeed in making one of their own, to borrow the ensign from the British merchant marine.
Is it because the United Kingdom considered our Canadian troops merely as mercenaries of the proud Albion? Were our troops considered as mere merchandise that could be sold to a country at war? True Canadians are still puzzled in regard to the spirit which inspired this selection. Since then questions are constantly being asked that give rise to much controversy. For lack of a sounder argument we were told that the situation was temporary.
However, Mr. Speaker, we find that what was to be temporary is taking a permanent character, and our men continue to fight for liberty, under the auspices of mercantilism.
However, it was indeed mentioned in the house that such loan was only temporary. Hence I am surprised to hear this group clamouring to appropriate an object which had only been loaned. In life I was always taught that other people's property had to be returned; this property may have been very useful to us since many French Canadians today have gone to meet their Maker, after having been good servants during their lifetime.
In my opinion the red ensign now deserves to be returned to its owners.
The government offers us the design of a new distinctive flag, of a really Canadian flag, in the true sense of the word. This government has certainly not selected this design lightly. We ourselves presented a distinctive design, but we bowed before the opinion of the majority, and, in order not to delay any longer the debate on the various designs, in the interest of the country, we have foregone our own selection so that the design proposed by the government would be unanimously endorsed.
Now that the debate on the design has come to a close, the official opposition demands a referendum on the acceptance of this same design, and pretends that the people have not been consulted.

Stop making us laugh with your ridiculous buffooneries which mean nothing, but still the country has to pay for such unheard of childish debates.
The Canadian people have requested a distinctive flag for a hundred years. Indeed, in 1945, in order to satisfy the desires of the people, the government decided to borrow the ensign of the British merchant marine, pending the time it would be in a position to decide on its own design.
To ask a popular consultation is precisely the Conservative way of sending into oblivion a proposal which that party was never honest enough to present to the Canadian people, when 98 per cent of the province of Quebec and almost 80 per cent of the people in Canada as a whole instructed us, at the last election, to give Canada a distinctive flag.
In such a case would we be going back to our constituents to get permission they already gave us? This is sheer nonsense. In my opinion, to ask for a referendum on a question when 100 per cent of my electors gave me a clear and precise mandate would be evidence of obvious inefficiency.
What are the motives of a group of Anglo-Saxons and a few new Canadians who do not understand yet the meaning of the words "Canadian-bi-ethnical", who have not understood yet that it is time to get out of mythological colonialism and have not realized that Canada is now an adult country?
Perhaps we will never know, it is probably because they remained in Canada without really belonging here.
They are somewhat like the husband who could never leave his mother for his wife. The story goes on to say that he finally divorced.
I do not even dare to think that any group among them could take action to kill right off a measure of such importance to Canada, because they would show the whole world that they are traitors to their country.
I was listening the other day to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who was saying how the government of the day had held a plebiscite concerning conscription in 1942. He added that that plebiscite had done justice to Canada. I will not discuss that question which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle fully outlined, because 76 per cent of Quebeckers voted against conscription.
This means that the 1942 conscription did not do justice, as mentioned by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. Indeed, a plebiscite

or referendum, just like the popular vote, is very much influenced, not to say more by all the political factors.
However, with regard to the comparison made in the house by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, I maintain that the present question is not at all the same as the situation which existed in 1942. In fact, in 1942 the government of the day had explicitly promised, with the evident purpose of being elected, not to impose conscription. After being elected, it remembered that finance had its rights and that it was stronger than governments. Reneging on their most solemn election promises, this government, admitting defeat before the giants of finance, had no alternative but to go once more to the people asking to be freed from its undertaking.
Indeed, the people had not voted for the military and the government which was elected in 1942 was not committed to impose conscription. On the contrary, its terms of reference being quite clear, it had to promise the people not to launch this country into the blazing furnace of war.
That is why a referendum was called for at the time. Whereas today this government made the flag one of the main planks of its platform in the last election.
We, of the Ralliement Creditiste promised our voters to support without reserve any government which would have the courage of presenting a distinctive flag to the house. We now have this distinctive flag design, for which we were elected. What else do we want, Mr. Speaker?
Our party is in favour of immediate and concrete decisions. We are not a group of puppets, but a group determined to do something for Canada, if it is not too late.
We say that now is the time for Canada to have its own flag, and not a borrowed one.
We are proud to see that 75 per cent of the members, Anglo-Saxon, Canadian or new Canadian, are prepared to support the proposed flag. I say to the house that this may be the first indication that we are really on the way toward achieving Canadian unity.
It may be argued that there are still some opponents in the house. This only proves the rule. We should not take offence at that fact, because there will always be some opponents, even if it is only to preserve the seed of colonialism planted in Canada 300 years ago. We should not give them more importance than they deserve.
Canadian Flag
Similarly, we, from Quebec, hear with some satisfaction the loud protests of a small group.
In fact, for years Quebeckers have been accused of being separatists, of wanting to destroy confederation and now with the introduction of a really distinctive flag, the true enemies of Canadian unity come out of the shadows. Now the country will know who does not want any understanding in Canada. And you can imagine that it is not French Canadians.
What a scandal to have thus shown their petty secular game. You can see those who have always remained riveted to one-way traditions, without ever officially considering the two ethnic groups making up Canada.
That is why I was very sorry to hear a new Canadian who claimed the other day that he was speaking on behalf of his group. Poor fellow. As a latecomer, he still has a lot, not to say everything to learn, since he has not yet grasped the meaning of the democratic system in Canada. Imbued with the socialism of countries behind the iron curtain, they are unable to understand the democratic freedoms, because in a democratic country they live without realizing it, like socialists, like integrationists.
I fear there are still too many of those new Canadians, and even some Anglo-Saxons, who are unable to take their adult life seriously. It would be time for them to examine their conscience.
Speaking on the amendment, the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Lamb) expressed the fear that each province might have its own flag.
Earlier an hon. member stated that the new flag might favour especially the French Canadians, which is totally incorrect since, at the present time, many more Anglo-Saxons than French Canadians are in favour of that flag which pleases me greatly. It indicates that this flag design will foster unity in Canada and that we are fighting for the recognition of the two great ethnic groups in our country.
Someone said earlier that in his province French Canadians faced no problems. I quite believe it; it is forbidden to speak French on the labour market. Look at what goes on in those provinces and you will see that the English and the new Canadians do not dare to try to understand the difficulties experienced by those French Canadians who want to keep their language. And then they come to us and tell us matter of factly: We have no

Canadian Flag
problems with French Canadians in our province. Of course not because they have been integrated for 50 or 60 years; we have seen it in the case of the Acadians who have become integrated. The French Canadian does not want to become integrated and I wonder if that will be understood some day.
I suggest to some people in those English speaking provinces to reflect briefly at night on the situation of that ethnic group. We have a Canada made up of two ethnic groups, and I wonder if the new Canadians will finally understand that country because when French Canadians are obliged to attend English schools, to use English at work and before the courts, where everything is done in English, they tell us: We do not have any problem with French Canadians in our province. Of course not, because they are patient, much more patient than some groups which today are up in arms because there is talk of adopting a national flag for the whole of Canada.
It will be necessary to search our souls, to come back to our senses and to ask ourselves what is a Canadian, a true Canadian? A true Canadian, as I said a little earlier, is somewhat like a husband. He must leave his mother, his father, in short his native land.
If we want to build a Canada worthy of every Canadian, whatever his origin may be, as long as you keep on creating here mother-country images, you will not be true Canadians. And that might be because you never had the opportunity to make sacrifices to deserve this Canadianism. We shall have to dispel those images and get down to work, because there has been enough talk about such myths. It is high time to think like the true Canadians that you are and that you should all be in this house.
Frankly, I am shocked to see those groups hanging on doggedly to the red ensign, which they admire because it was loaned to us, because it served our purpose and it was all we had. However, we should decide to give it back. It is all very well to be patient, and I think England has been very patient, but today she must be given back what belongs to her. Today we have a government that had the courage to offer a flag to the nation. Although we do not agree that it is 100 per cent representative of Canada, we abide by the decision and say: this is our flag and we shall fully support it.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. With

regard to those of us who have spoken for the retention of the red ensign in this debate, the hon. member has said that we do not understand their position and he cannot understand our taking a position in favour of the retention of the red ensign. He has also said he is for the unification of all parts of Canada. I would like to ask him if he ascribes to the views of the leader of his party, who said when making a statement not too long ago:
Real Caouette, the deputy leader of the Social Credit party, admitted that he admired Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini for their political qualities. Mr. Caouette said also that he had refused to fight in the second world war because "...I didn't think Canada had given me anything worth fighting for".

I	rise	on a	question	of
privilege-

I want to finish my question. Does the hon. member not agree that the very principles he is putting forth are those used by the dictators	in	this world	to conquer
other countries?

I	rise	on a	question	of
privilege, Mr. Speaker-

I	am very glad that,	at
last, that voice should make itself heard. I am asked why we blame supporters of the red ensign. I thought I had made myself clear, but they still do not understand.
I maintain that we have no right to take what belongs to somebody else. We may borrow it, but we cannot keep it for ourselves. It would be an insult to Great Britain to keep her merchant marine flag as we are doing now. I feel it is a mere question of justice to hand it back to her, since today we are being offered a distinctive and exclusively Canadian flag. We do not want the red ensign, but we want a symbol to represent us, something truly Canadian. It seems to me everyone should understand that.
As far as Hitler and Mussolini are concerned, I want to point out to the hon. member that he is absolutely out of order. I think the hon. member is only trying to call attention to himself. If he had only read the whole statement of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), when he spoke about Hitler and Mussolini, he would have understood but in my opinion, he will never understand. He should have read the complete text instead of taking two or three sentences out of it-because you know that you can have somebody hung for two or three words

taken out of context. I will go even further and say that in the better days of Mussolini, priests made us kneel down and pray for his victory. And today we would condemn him because he made a mistake? Mr. Speaker, if we were to condemn every person in this house who has made a mistake, there would not be a single member left.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I appreciate that the hon. member for Roberval is trying to reply to the question put to him by the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb), but since the discussion between the two hon. gentlemen is not related to the resolution under consideration, I would suggest that he limit his remarks to the subject of the present debate.
Mr. Speaker, you allowed the question and I thought that I was entitled to reply. Since I have to give a complete answer, I wonder if you would permit me to finish.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I say to the hon. member that his reply is quite adequate in my opinion. Consequently, I would suggest that he does not pursue the discussion any further.
Mr. Speaker, you are a better judge than I am. I felt that my reply was incomplete but you do not think so. That is not too bad.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I certainly will not tolerate being called in any circumstance a "follower of Mussolini and Hitler", especially if it is the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac who does the name-calling. May I say that that is usually known as a dirty blow, a punch below the belt. To my mind, there is but one way to protect oneself from such attacks and such name-calling tactics, and I advise the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac to look up the dictionary for the meaning of the words "distinctive flag", which really mean distinctive in the first instance.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that other members do not resort to such name-calling tactics as I feel that there is not a single member of this house who deserves such treatment, not even the member who indulged in this practice.

Mr. Speaker, there are possibly two main reasons why I hope my remarks will be somewhat
Canadian Flag
brief today. One is the fact that there has already been considerable debate on this issue, and many times it has become rather acrimonious. The second reason is that nothing that has been said in this house these past days will be likely to change anyone's opinion particularly. I think that possibly each and every member has studied the matter for himself or herself and arrived at the point where he or she knows what the decision will be as far as they are concerned. Therefore there may not be too much to be accomplished by lengthy debate.
Thinking back over the last few weeks it is easy to remember all of the questions which have been asked relating to the flag issue; the intention of the government with respect to the introduction of the resolution, the nature of the designs they were going to advocate, and the objective as far as its place on the agenda of the house was concerned. Therefore I think that even though the debate has possibly been of short duration as far as the formal debate is concerned, it has already occupied a considerable part of the attention of the house.
I appreciated very much the interesting remarks made by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) this morning. I would say that I agree with him. I think the implication of his remarks was to the effect that the silence on the part of many with respect to certain trends in Canada today has given undue encouragement to extremists who do not appreciate the feelings and the convictions of Canadians from coast to coast. When hon. members rise in this house and insinuate that those who are opposing this particular resolution and the adoption of a new flag are not true Canadians and prefer to remain in a state of colonial immaturity, I think it indicates a complete lack of understanding of the basic concepts of Canadianism. The purpose of the resolution before us, no matter what may be said to the contrary, is to change our national symbol.
I was somewhat disappointed by the words the other day of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) when he said in concluding his remarks-I have already indicated that I have the highest regard for the hon. member and usually a great deal of respect for his judgment-that Canada has not got a national flag. Then he went on to give some quotations to substantiate that assertion. I do not believe that that is entirely so. Perhaps technically we can say that Canada does not have a flag, but in reality Canada does have a flag, and has had a flag always. And no

Canadian Flag
matter what sneering interventions are made from my left-we are getting used to those here-that is a fact. The world recognizes that fact, for we know that wherever Canadians dwell and are represented the Canadian red ensign is recognized as the Canadian flag. It flies from national buildings, from our embassies, and, as I have said, wherever there is Canadian representation. Therefore to all intents and purposes Canada has had a flag and does have a flag.
Furthermore, if Canada does not have a flag, why is it that national organizations have taught our children the significance of the red ensign or the union jack? I received a letter from a scholar the other day, and he pointed out that in the various organizations to which school children belong they have been taught the significance of this flag. Therefore, if Canada does not have a flag, why is it that our young people have been reared with the idea in mind that we do have a flag and have been taught what it stands for? I am sure that those who have accepted Canadian citizenship in this country have recognized that we have a flag. It has been used at ceremonies and has been recognized and acknowledged as the Canadian flag.
I say again that this resolution is not to adopt a distinctive flag but to change our national flag. The question is asked: Where do Canadians stand on this question? We know where some stand. There are others who believe that we have to get rid of what to them are the objectionable features which they see as symbols of colonialism.
Agreed.

I hear hon. members to my left say "Agreed". Well, we know where they stand. They are speaking for the radical, fanatical element in Canada and we know what to expect from them. Nevertheless there are those who believe, on the other hand, that we should retain at any cost the present symbols which are indicative of our rich heritage, whether it be French or English or that of any other nation.
United Canada loyalists.
Keep it up. I should think your stock is dropping considerably in the province of Quebec; so keep it up.
And yours.

Well, we will see after the next election, no doubt. As I was saying, where do Canadians stand on this particular

issue? I do not think there has been any attempt to ascertain what is the consensus across the country. Therefore, before we move in the direction of changing our national symbol, I think there should be some understanding as to what the Canadian people as a whole want. Whatever it is, I think we have the right to know.
What is the procedure which has thus far been followed in achieving this objective of changing our national symbol? We have been referred many times to the matter of the Liberal election promises, and some have suggested that the government were elected on the basis of this particular promise. I do not think that is absolutely true. There is no doubt that this promise was included in their platform, but nevertheless I do not think they can say that they were elected on the basis of their promise to provide a distinctive national flag for Canada. As pointed out by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), there is perhaps a difference of opinion as to what "distinctive" means. The order in council to which he refers does refer to the Canadian ensign as a distinctive national flag. Others would take it that it means something entirely different and that it does not show anything of our heritage. It does not show anything of our racial origin but is something strictly and absolutely indicative of Canada today. Therefore, that is the beginning of this particular issue, the Liberals having made this particular promise in the election campaign.
On April 17 the Prime Minister, in reply to a question which was asked of him, stated that the Liberals had promised that within two years Canada would have a distinctive national flag, and he said that the government had been in office for one year. I think anyone who is absolutely honest would have to say that the Prime Minister meant to leave the impression that there was not any undue haste to bring this particular matter before parliament. I do not think we should draw any other inference.
Then shortly after that we find there is a distinct change. I should like to refer to an editorial in one of my local papers, the Fraser Valley Record for May 22 last, and I will just read about two paragraphs from it:
While, like the Royal Canadian Legion, we see no need to change Canada's flag, the red ensign with the Canadian coat of arms in the field, the objective viewpoint of a friendly observer below our border is of timely interest...
"Mr. Pearson has been in no hurry to redeem his party's pledge to adopt a new flag. Caution is the word, and properly so.

A country's flag, no matter how aesthetically offensive it may be to some people, is something more than a design. It embodies, as can no other symbol, a nation's past, present and future even when, in Canada, it has never been officially adopted. It flies in the hearts of a nation."
Perhaps I should clarify that particular statement. It is a quotation from a newspaper published in Portland, Oregon. It says the Prime Minister is wise in taking his time because of the implications of this problem.
It was not too long after this that the whole situation changed. As we know, the Prime Minister introduced his resolution and the situation developed from there on. What happened to change the Prime Minister's intention so suddenly in this regard? This began as a matter which appeared to be of not too great urgency. It developed into one of urgent priority. I wonder who the right hon. gentleman's advisers were? I wonder where the pressure came from. I wonder what made him change his mind so rapidly and so abruptly.
We all remember the lengthy list of legislative items which he himself presented to us for consideration. Again, it was the Prime Minister himself who indicated his belief that these items should be disposed of as expeditiously as possible. I will not read that particular list; it is a lengthy one. Nevertheless, we found that suddenly the whole thing was reversed and an entirely new item of business appeared, one which was to take priority over practically everything else.
Anyway, the flag resolution was introduced. The Prime Minister said there was to be a free vote. What do we mean by a free vote? Everybody knows what a free vote is. It is a vote which gives every member an opportunity to present an opinion dictated by his conscience, without any serious repercussions attaching to the result of the diversion. We accepted that statement in good faith. We believed the Prime Minister meant what he said. But it seems he did not, because not too long afterwards he made it clear that though everybody, even Liberal members, could vote according to their consciences-they would not be read out of the party

the government intended to treat the matter as a question of confidence and, if it was repeated, there would be another general election. I suggest this is a complete repudiation of the principle of a free vote.
What came next? The right hon. gentleman came into the house and challenged the opposition to bring in a want of confidence motion based on the flag issue. My only com-
Canadian Flag
ment is this: The Prime Minister for some reason reduced this issue from one which should have been maintained on a high level of debate to a political football by threatening members of this house and the people in general that they would have to face another protracted and expensive election campaign unless they agreed to the proposal he was making. The objective of this resolution may be distasteful to many but the procedures which are being followed are infuriating Canadians right across this nation.
I do not intend to make any personal attack on the Prime Minister. We have looked upon him as a diplomat and as a statesman. He has been recognized as such around the world.
Hear, hear.

I am just going to say this- I think members opposite must be applauding what I am about to say now: I believe the image of the Prime Minister as a statesman and a diplomat will be badly besmirched because of the way in which this political issue is being handled. That is the opinion of a good many people. I believe this debate should continue for the present so that the pros and cons may be clearly set forth in this chamber. I believe every member should have the opportunity to present his views and the views of his constituents in this regard, whether they be for or against the motion. But, having said that, I believe that after there has been sufficient debate on this matter to bring out all the relevant facts there should be agreement to take no final decision but to allow time for reflection both by members of this house and by the Canadian people.
We ought to get along with the other matters the Prime Minister has mentioned. I do not think we can brag about what has been accomplished this session. We have made some progress, but I do not think we have made sufficient progress. In this connection I should like to read the first and the last paragraphs of an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of June 29:
Rarely in Canadian history has parliament presented such an unattractive picture of itself to the people who elect it, the people who pay for it, the people whose public business it is supposed to transact.
The voters are not amused, the voters are not at all impressed, with what they see in Ottawa. It is in the knowledge of this public distaste and disillusion-
This refers to the results of a proposal the Prime Minister made.

Canadian Flag
-that the various house leaders, when they meet today, should find some method to get parliament back on the rails.
As I said, I believe there should be every opportunity given for members to present their views on this subject, both for and against. Then, in my opinion, the matter should be shelved and we should proceed to consider other items of business. Later, perhaps in the fall, the Prime Minister could give serious thought to the suggestion of a referendum. This is, of course, the subject of the amendment, but I wish to point out that it is not original in any way because my hon. friend from Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) spoke as follows on February 27, as reported in Hansard on page 315:
I should like to make a few remarks about this business of a national flag. We really get into deep water when we start talking about a national flag, I realize that. I think the solution lies in having a committee set up which will choose perhaps four or five designs out of the some 2,500 or 2,900 designs that have been submitted, and put these on a ballot. They should include the red ensign, and should be put to a referendum of the people, with a transferable vote so that each individual would choose the first, second, third, fourth and fifth in the order he preferred and, by the process of elimination, we will then have over 50 per cent of the people voting in favour of a particular flag. That will take all of us off the hook and put the responsibility where it belongs, on the shoulders of the people.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment introduced by the official opposition represents nothing new because my colleague, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe), suggested the same thing as early as February 27. If we are to have a new flag, Mr. Speaker, let us have one of which Canadians can be proud and not one about which the best thing that can be said is that nobody else has it.
I suggest there are scores and hundreds- I could go higher than that-there are multitudes of people in this nation who want a new flag but they do not want the one that is the choice of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). They agree that we should have something else, but with regard to the one he has put forward they wonder why in the world he chose it and submitted it for the consideration of cabinet and then to the House of Commons. That applies to Liberals as well as to a lot of other people. They just do not like it.
I am going to conclude by making the plea once again that, no matter where we stand on this issue, we should have ample opportunity to present our views and arguments, that there should then be a cooling off period or time for reflection, after which we can then

come back and make a decision that will be intelligent and in the interests of the unity of this great nation of which we are all proud to form a part.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this historic time in our history I should like to take the opportunity as the elected representative of the cosmopolitan constituency of Parkdale to plead with hon. members to seize this challenge and unique opportunity to ensure the unity of Canada by showing a better understanding of our parliamentary procedures and by also demonstrating their good will to co-operate and show Canada that we here are responsible in the exercise of our duties.
Many speeches have been made in this chamber on this issue. Some of them, I am sorry to say, were not very praiseworthy. Some speakers preceding me have even demeaned the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of this country or his intentions as far as the Canadian flag resolution is concerned. Let me remind these hon. members that we are proceeding in this debate according to our parliamentary rules, that the Canadian flag resolution of the government was put on the order paper on May 28 and that members of parliament have had time to read, study and reflect upon the resolution since May 28. It was not debated immediately. It was only on June 15 that the Prime Minister introduced the resolution with his historic speech and since June 15 we have had ample time to express our opinions on the government's resolution concerning a distinctive Canadian flag.
It is the Prime Minister, I am happy to say, who has proven his Canadian patriotism and his courage by his decisions and by the speeches he has made in this chamber and throughout our country in order to strengthen Canadian confederation and therefore our national unity. Since the Prime Minister's historic address in the House of Commons on December 17, 1962, when he declared that confederation was our declaration of faith in the destiny of a united Canada, he has rallied Canadians to the cause of renewing our efforts and rededicating ourselves to our greatest national cause, our national purpose, a strong and united Canada.
This government's enviable record of important bills and other proposed legislation now on the order paper demonstrates the sincerity and determination of the Prime Minister's goal which he described on April 23, 1963, to the Canadian nation in his first television address after taking office, that

although our task in the second session of Canada's twenty sixth parliament is indeed complex, "it is time to excite the daring, to test the strong and to give new promise to the timid". He went on to say:
It will indeed be a time of direction and of decision, when our efforts are sustained, our purpose clear, and our faith high.
The Canadian government's decision in the flag resolution we are now debating is exciting, it is daring and it is testing many timid people. The beautiful design proposed by the government, consisting of three red maple leaves joined on one stem across a white background with blue vertical borders, has its historic and heraldic significance. I regret to say that many members of this chamber refuse to understand that there are elements of history and elements of heraldic significance in the design proposed by the Canadian government.
The historic element in this flag dates back to May 26, 1868, when Queen Victoria issued a royal warrant establishing the great seal of Canada and the arms of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. This seal, a sprig of three maple leaves, appeared twice. For Ontario the emblem granted was three gold maple leaves on a green background and for Quebec the emblem was three green maple leaves on a gold background. Later, Mr. Speaker, King George V also gave Canada other emblems and symbols of which we are proud.
I am certain that the proposed design, Mr. Speaker, has the support of the majority of Canadians. This majority is reflected also by majority support for this resolution as members of the House of Commons take their stand one after the other.
Many of my constituents have expressed their support of this distinctive Canadian flag. Every day young Canadians are enthusiastically expressing their acceptance and admiration of the maple leaf flag. Canadians of all backgrounds and origins have voiced their support for the new flag.
For the information of many hon. members who have requested it, and especially for the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), may I say first of all that if they would take the trouble to read the reports of the ethnic press in Canada they would learn that the Estonian newspaper Meie Elu indicates that Estonians want to see Canada as a completely sovereign country with her own symbols, a flag and an anthem. The German weekly Der Courier states that it is hoped there will be a ma-
Canadian Flag
jority who will accept the government's design. The Ukrainian weekly, New Pathway, stated that Canada should have her own distinctive flag, and the design is certainly the right one. The Ukrainian Voice states that no damage would be done if the new flag were not adopted at present.
Beside this evidence from the ethnic press throughout Canada, there are also ethnic organizations which have expressed their support for the Canadian flag as proposed by this government. Last year a delegation of the young Slavic alliance came to a hearing of the royal commission on biculturalism and bilingualism. They also voiced their support for the new, distinctive Canadian flag. The national executive of the Canadian Polish congress representing over 400,000 Canadians of Polish origin in this country came out strongly in a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag.
This overwhelming evidence, Mr. Speaker, for a new Canadian flag proved also that a plebiscite on this matter is needless. As was so ably argued and proven by so many members in this house, a referendum or plebiscite is not in keeping with our British parliamentary system. A plebiscite on the subject would not serve national unity. We members of parliament were sent here to make decisions, to legislate and to carry out the mandate of the Canadian electorate. Canada must have her own and distinctive flag because Canadians want to rally round a symbol to pursue their national purpose across this country. I am sure we all want a flag that can qualify as a truly national flag. The maple leaf design of the Canadian government is a truly national flag, representing our historic past, representing our exciting present. I am sure it will also represent the glorious future of Canada.
In accepting a new Canadian flag, Mr. Speaker, we will accept also the union jack as proof of our loyalty to the monarch of Canada and our very close association with the British commonwealth of nations. We respect the union jack and we respect also the red ensign. We will respect a new, distinctive Canadian flag. I am sure that as responsible members of parliament we will respect the maple leaf flag if it is approved by parliament and that we shall do so, not only for ourselves, but for our beloved children and for Canada, our home and native land.

May I ask a question of the hon. member? I have heard him mention

Canadian Flag
"Canadian unity". Some Conservative members have used these words "Canadian unity". May I know what the hon. member's definition is of this word "unity"?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In response to the hon. member who asked this question I may say that, to me, unity means one national purpose designed to achieve the best life for all of us in Canada. Unity also means harmonious relationships between all the people in Canada, harmonious relationships between all the provincial governments in Canada. Unity, Mr. Speaker, also means unity of action in order that we may play a proud role in the international field.
Then, I conclude, that for the hon. member unity means only unity of purpose and not of races or groups?

Why don't you make
your own speech?

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this important debate I believe history is being made today in this honourable chamber. I cannot say that I agree altogether with the remarks of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) when he stated that it was an exciting debate. Indeed this morning when asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) about the resolution on the flag, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) referred to it as a simple resolution. Far from being a simple resolution, I am sure it is a resolution that requires the utmost soul-searching for every member in this house.
Little did I realize that the day would come when I would have to rise in my place in this chamber and defend the Canadian red ensign as Canada's national flag. I have long looked upon it as Canada's national flag, just as thousands of other Canadians have. Here we have before us a resolution asking parliament to replace it with another flag. The day before yesterday, Mr. Speaker, many members of this house as well as thousands of Canadians had an opportunity of witnessing a display of pageantry on the lawn in front of the parliament buildings. This was as fine a display as has ever been held on the hill. This program was relayed to millions of Canadians by means of television so that they, too, would be able to fill their hearts with pride. The 66 Canadian red ensigns fluttering in the breeze made a most impressive appearance. I am likewise sure that my good friends from Quebec must have had their hearts filled with pride by this program.

Two days ago we celebrated Canada's 97th birthday. Birthdays are times when we look back over the past years. They give us a chance to realize those things which we in this country have done or have left undone. July 3 is a day on which Canadians like to fly the flag. 1 should like to quote from an editorial that appeared in the Telegram of June 30:

As I was saying before, the past year has been a year in which members of this house and the fortunate citizens of this country of Canada have wondered whether this country could find the unity to endure, or would it fall into separate parts only to be gobbled up by the great republic to the south? Mackenzie King in his wisdom knew better than to promote the idea of a distinctive Canadian flag. He did, however, proclaim the Canadian red ensign as the official flag to be flown from all federal buildings either within or without Canada. Our soldiers fought under it and died under it; and at the risk of it being said that I am repetitious I should like to refer to the words of the distinguished commander, General Crerar, of the first Canadian army when he returned to Ottawa at the

close of the second world war and was graciously honoured by then prime minister Mackenzie King. Generally speaking, Canadians have appeared to be very happy to go along with the Canadian red ensign. But no, the Prime Minister, for political expediency and to fulfil a political promise, has pressed the issue of a national flag. I ask, Mr. Speaker, who is it who has pressed for this new flag? At their recent session, the council of the corporation of the county of Wellington passed a resolution recommending the adoption of the Canadian red ensign as the national flag of the Dominion of Canada.
This resolution was circulated to all the county councils in Ontario and I am told that over 50 per cent of them endorsed the resolution and showed their approval.
I think it might be worth while putting on record one or two observations made by constituents of mine, residents of the city of Guelph. An inquiring reporter of the Guelph Mercury took a tour of the main streets of the city and asked several people what they thought of the new flag, its design and its colours, and I should like to read a few of the replies. I will not mention the constituents by name although their names are given in this report. The first one said:
"War ravished countries would put something like this out when they are trying to save paint"... She felt the new flag was very conservative and that because the English element is our strongpoint, the British flag should be kept flying.
Another said:
"If Canada should have a new flag...it should at least have a definite Canadian identification and not maple leaves. Maple trees grow, among other places, both in Missouri and Yugoslavia. Moreover, why should the leaves be red? And they are of poor design".
A local medical doctor replied that he definitely did not like the new flag. The report continues:

He said from a heraldic angle it is incorrect. The blue bars should be horizontal and not vertical. He said that the unity that Canadians look for will not be achieved by producing a flag of this type.
"Ethnic groups coming to Canada were happy to accept Canada as they found her. There was no arrangement whereby they understood the flag would be changed. This act of expediency will not, in my opinion, lead to greater unity. If, at a later date, Quebec becomes independent, Canada will have gained nothing from this act, but will be left with a flag depicting three wilting maple leaves and a white surrender background."
As a Canadian citizen he acknowledged the need for a new flag but thought the decision had materialized too rapidly to take into consideration the feelings of the people.

He has succeeded only in creating disunity.

The great flag flap at a glance:
a.	Press says P.M. has decided on flag with three red maple leaves on white, with blue bars at either side.

That describes the type of muddle in which we find ourselves at the present time. I cannot help accusing this government and the Prime Minister of partisan propaganda of the worst sort. He is attempting to use his power and the prestige of his office as Prime Minister to supplant an authorized national flag with a design which has neither the full support of his own party nor of the House of Commons and the people of Canada as a whole. By his arbitrary action, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the Prime Minister of this country is setting faction against faction,
[Mr. Hales.1
party against party and, I am fearful, region against region. This is the unhappy state to which the Prime Minister has reduced us and the people of Canada.
There has never been a prime minister since confederation who has caused so much strife, bitterness, disunity and confusion. I for one, and I am sure every member of this house must share this view and resent the Prime Minister's tactics in holding a club over the heads of members by saying: "No holiday or recess until you have passed my flag resolution; accept my new flag design or there will be an election". The right hon. gentleman must know that the people of Canada do not want an election at this time after two elections in a little more than three years. I should like to read in this connection an article which appeared in the Guelph Mercury. It says, referring to the Prime Minister:
He seems bent on bulldozing a new flag through the Commons in a frame of truculence worthy of C.D. Howe during the pipe line debate in 1956. This is the way in which this once great diplomat and statesman has handled such a delicate question. Is this the way democracy should function? The dictatorial manner of handling this flag issue will long be remembered by the people of Canada. The Liberal government muzzled this parliament at the time of the pipe line debate but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada are not going to be muzzled on this flag issue. The Prime Minister even took it into his own hands to fly his flag out on the front lawn on parliament hill. Four weeks ago, to the day, I rose in my place to propose a course of action under standing order No. 26. To adjourn this house so as to consider a matter of urgent national importance-not to debate the flag issue, because that was to be debated the following Monday, but to debate a question of principle, namely whether the No. 1 Canadian citizen, the Prime Minister of this country, should ignore, circumvent and sidestep a piece of legislation, a law, an order in council which was passed on September 5, 1945 and which definitely states that no flag should be flown from

government property or on occasions or places until such time as the house should approve a new flag.
What did the Prime Minister do? Not only did he fly the flag between five o'clock and eight o'clock but at the request of some hon. members on my left he flew it from one o'clock to two o'clock in order that they might see it before catching the four o'clock train home. In my view his action in this regard was both arrogant and unlawful.
What about the clever manoeuver of printing a postage stamp with a replica of the new flag design on it weeks before that flag was introduced into this house? It was a clever manoeuver on the part of the government; a means by which this emblem was circulated throughout Canada. They flew a kite, and what a kite it was. As the drinks were served and the newspapermen nibbled on sandwiches, Mr. Pearson brought out several flag designs on cardboards, selected one with a cluster of three maple leaves and two blue bands and placed it on the mantelpiece as his choice. He said he was prepared to have the government stand or fall on the maple leaf flag. The Prime Minister was careful however to make clear that the flag on the mantel was his personal choice.

How much more sensible and more democratic it would have been to have set up a non-partisan committee of this house charged with the responsibility of submitting to parliament a design for a new national flag, not one introduced by a political party but one chosen by parliament.
What do we have? We have a flag which appears to have been proposed by the government in the same light hearted manner as the original Canadian pension plan was conceived, in the absence of careful thought

or the expert advice which is available to any government. Yes, if ever a serious matter was badly handled, this is it. It is thrust upon us. We are being put under pressure. The people of these communities appreciate the right to express their opinions through a plebiscite. I am quite sure they do not claim that the elected members of these municipal councils are derelict in their duty when they decide to hold a plebiscite.
