So far as the issue of a new flag is concerned and the viewpoint of my riding, I am prepared to vote against the new flag and support the Canadian red ensign. My decision was reached by consultation with many constituents. Out of every 100 letters I have received, 90 were in favour of retaining the red ensign and 10 in favour of a new flag but not necessarily the flag submitted by the government. The newspaper poll in my riding showed 66 per cent in favour of the Canadian red ensign. My other reasons, of course, involve my own personal choice or decision on the matter.
I think it should be of interest to the house to realize what the outcome was of a poll taken by 29 newspapers across Canada. Only two newspapers recorded a majority in support of a new distinctive flag. As of June
5	last these were the results. On the prairies
6	newspapers took part, gathering 9,968 votes, with 65 per cent supporting the red ensign. In Ontario and Quebec 14 newspapers participated, with a total of 53,424 votes recorded, 52 per cent being in favour of the red ensign. In the maritimes 5 newspapers took part with 1,466 votes being cast and 69.09 per cent being in favour of the red ensign. That was the picture across Canada on June 5.
Yesterday the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) spoke in this debate and she brought up the question of voting according to the wishes of the constituency she represents. She gave us the impression that she had spoken to a good many people in her riding and that the maple leaf flag appeared to be the choice there. I did not believe that could be the case in that riding. I thought it rather strange and I made it my business to find out from the riding.
The Cobourg Sentinel-Star, the largest newspaper in Northumberland county, conducted a poll of its readers and published the results on May 27. The poll showed 24 in favour of the Canadian red ensign, 6 opposed to the red ensign and 5 undecided. In the opinion of Mr. Foster Russell, the publisher and editor of this journal, public opinion in Northumberland county is 65 to 70 per cent in favour of the red ensign. Yet the hon. lady said she felt the people there were in favour of the maple leaf flag. I think this is one of the greatest arguments there

can be that a referendum or plebiscite should be held in view of such a divergence of opinion. I was surprised when she said in her speech yesterday, as found on page 4949 of Hansard:
-I think we, as members of parliament, should look at this whole question regardless of our personal feelings in the matter, regardless even of what we think the majority of our constituents want.
I cannot imagine a member of parliament rising in his place and not voting the way the majority of his constituents want him to vote. I could perhaps understand the point if the design had been submitted by a committee but I think a different light is thrown on the matter altogether when the design has been approved and submitted by a political party. However, I give the hon. lady credit for rising in her place and speaking in this debate. I should like to hear from other members across the way. Could we not hear from the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Honey), the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown), the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene)? I see he is with us today. I know he has many other irons in the fire these days but maybe he will find the time to speak in the flag debate. What about the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis)? I see him in his place. We are both members of the public accounts committee and are good friends, I should like to hear him speak in the flag debate. Then there is the member for my neighbouring riding of Wentworth and my other neighbour, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley). What about the hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Temple)? I should like these gentlemen to rise and speak in this debate.
Have we heard from any of the front bench members on the other side? Have any of the cabinet ministers spoken in this debate? Why have they not risen in their places and given us their views? They should tell us now why they want this resolution and why they are supporting it. Let them rise in their places. I should like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) to rise and tell us their views. We should like to hear from them.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that there are rumours going around Canada, rumours that do not do any good whatever. They are rumours that should be hushed. We hear rumours to the effect the flag is being pushed

as a result of pressure from Quebec. These are things we hear. Is it to win votes in Quebec? We want to get answers to these questions. This loose talk is very harmful to Canada. It would be much better if these men would rise in their places now and set these rumours at rest.
However, I give the hon. lady full credit for rising in her place and speaking on this subject. I am at a loss to know why she would not be in favour of a plebiscite in view of the great conflict of opinion in her own riding. I dare say if some of these other members spoke and voted according to the opinion of their constituents they would have to vote, not with their party but with us.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.
What about the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), and some of these people?

They will have their turn, and no doubt they will take their turn. I think the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) might express his views as well. We agree on some things, but there are times when I do not agree with him. I do not agree with the great paradox we find when he is urging people to grow tobacco and his minister is spending money telling people not to use it.
I must proceed or my time will be exhausted. Mr. Abbott-and this might be repetitious-when he spoke in this house on the matter of holding a plebiscite on conscription in 1942, a very honourable member of the Liberal party, had this to say:
It seems to me no useful purpose is going to be served by an interminable debate in this house or outside it as to the desirability or otherwise of this plebiscite. We are going to have it-
He talks like a real Liberal.
-and in spite of what some people may say it is a thoroughly democratic procedure. I spoke a moment ago about responsibility and I suggest that the people of the country as a whole now have an opportunity to assume their responsiblity, to turn out and vote and show each other and the rest of the world, if you will, that democracy can be made to work even in wartime.
They took a plebiscite in wartime, so surely we can take time in peacetime to let the people speak. There is no excuse in that regard. We cannot ignore the many minority groups that have such strong views on this new flag for Canada. What right has a minority government, and I remind you a
Canadian Flag
minority government is what you are, to railroad this flag through this house, ignoring the rights of those who feel very deeply on this matter? If this flag is pushed through now without hearing from them the rift will grow greater and greater.
It would be very simple and inexpensive to hold a plebiscite. It could be held at the time of the next federal election at little expense. You would simply walk in to vote, be given a ballot with the names of the candidates on it and you would be given another slip of paper with three or four flag designs in colour and you would simply mark an X opposite the one you preferred. I believe the method adopted in the province of Alberta, which is referred to as the transferable vote, could be adopted whereby you mark your choices first, second and third. There would be no problem in that regard. I know each Canadian would say, "I will be loyal to the flag which the majority of Canadians choose."
In conclusion, I review briefly what I have said. I suggest to the Prime Minister that if he is bound to bring in a new flag he should start over again with a clean sheet. He should set up a non-partisan committee to represent Canada and introduce a new design for parliamentary approval, not a government design. If he does not want to do that, he should withdraw the resolution that is before the house now. This is the last day of debate, at the moment. He should allow the members to reassess the whole issue during a summer recess. Let us go home to our constituencies; let us think about this very serious matter. Let it simmer a bit and then come back and decide where we go from there.
If these courses are not possible, then give the people of Canada an opportunity to express their views by means of a plebiscite. Surely out of these three suggestions the Prime Minister will find one that is acceptable, because he must understand the great damage that is being done to the country at this time. I hope he will choose the easiest course, and that is to pull this resolution off the order paper until next fall. Failing all this, surely a compromise is possible. A compromise can save this nation. A compromise is worth while. Let us do all we can to seek a compromise. I agree that the Canadian red ensign as it stands might not be entirely acceptable to everybody in Canada. I fully realize this. I think it is acceptable to the majority, but I may be wrong.

Canadian Flag
Surely the two great founding races of Canada can sit down and draft a flag design that will be acceptable to both. Each group will have to give up a little, this is certain. Each of these two great races is going to have to give and take a little in order to save this great nation. Surely a compromise can be reached in some way. In conclusion, I beg the Prime Minister and his government not to press the present design of a distinctive Canadian flag upon this house and the people of Canada.

should like to say a few words in support of the amendment which is before us and for the conducting of a referendum or plebiscite on this flag issue. At the outset, sir, I would like to say that unlike most of those who have spoken to date in favour of the referendum and in support of the red ensign, I personally am not of that number. I support the proposed maple leaf design. I hope to vote for that maple leaf flag design in a plebiscite in which other Canadians who oppose it may express their democratic right.
I am supporting this amendment and I intend to vote for it, if and when it comes to a vote. I hope that will be soon so that we can get on with the plebiscite and have this decision made. I should like to commend the Prime Minister of this country upon the introduction of this maple leaf flag design. I think he has done well. However, I do not agree with his methods in trying to establish it as the flag of Canada.
I do not think that he or his government, or this parliament, has any mandate from the people of Canada to change the flag. So far as I know the nation is still uncommitted on that very important question. Therefore I feel that the amendment calling for a poll of the people on the flag is the very essence of democracy, and I support it.
I do not intend to spend much time in advancing my arguments in favour of the maple leaf design. I will simply say that I think Canada should have a flag which, when flown abroad, is distinguishable from all other countries' flags and which, when flown at home, will be an emblem which in time will function towards unifying the national community so that we can make Canada take a larger and better place in world affairs.
I should like to say a few words specifically in relation to the proposal for a plebiscite. In that regard I propose to discuss some of the arguments which have been advanced thus far against holding a plebiscite. One of these arguments is that it is not in the Cana-

dian or British tradition for us to take a plebiscite or referendum on such a question. Well, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of things in this country which were traditional in the past and which we have changed. There was the tradition held until not so many years ago that women should not have a vote. This is one tradition we got away from and it is good that we broke with it.
I do not put any particular weight on tradition for tradition's sake. A tradition should be studied to see what merit it has. If it is a good tradition, if it is realistic in the light of modern circumstances, then I believe we should retain it. If it is not then, like the traditions we have changed in the past, we should modify or do away with it. Therefore, I do not put any great faith or force in the argument of those opposed to having a plebiscite on the flag on the basis that it is not a British or Canadian tradition.
Another argument against the holding of a referendum on the flag is advanced, namely that it would serve to create acrimony from one end of the country to the other. No doubt there are strong feelings in the country, as there are in this house, on the matter of the flag. There are bound to be, but I personally have more faith in the Canadian people and in their common sense than to go along with those who argue that we cannot afford to put this matter up to the people. I think we can well afford to do that, and in the long run there will be no hard feelings such as will be created if we 265 members in this house take it upon ourselves to decide the opinions of 19 million people.
I think we should go ahead and let the people of Canada have a poll on this very basic general question of the flag, which is not a matter of business, or economics, or anything we can put down in black and white and argue in a mathematical fashion. Whatever kind of flag we favour, we should agree that a flag is a matter of spiritual emotion to all of us, that it is something on which everybody in Canada has the right to express his or her opinion, and I hope they are given that privilege.
It is said, Mr. Speaker, that the holding of a plebiscite is something that is very rarely done, that it is a difficult matter, and that it has many troublesome factors involved in it. More particularly it is said it is not usually done in British commonwealth countries. In this connection I would like to quote from the "Encyclopedia of Parliament", by Wilding, at page 486, in regard to referendums:
The machinery of the referendum has been used in a number of commonwealth countries-but not

In the United Kingdom-to obtain for the government a direct decision from the electorate on a specific subject involving legislation, and parliamentary voters are entitled to express their opinion by voting for or against the government's proposition. The referendum has been used in Canada and New Zealand on the question of prohibition, and in Australia to introduce amendments to the constitution. A referendum was also held in Southern Rhodesia in 1953 which decided that the colony would form a federation with Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
From that we can see it is not an unusual thing in British commonwealth procedure to take a matter such as a flag or other major problem to the people and let them decide it themselves.
The idea of the plebiscite or referendum, or polling of the people, comes down to us from very ancient times. There is an old, old saying that goes something like this, "On minor matters the few decide; on great affairs the many." I think we should keep that in mind, that over many centuries many great problems, such as a flag issue, have been settled by putting the question directly to the people directly affected.
There is nothing difficult or particularly onerous about holding a plebiscite. I have in mind the instructions for the holding of a referendum prepared by the returning referendum official in 1942, explaining in detail how a plebiscite should be conducted, where, and who should be employed. It has been done, and can be done again.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote very briefly from a British statesman of some note, the late Sir Austen Chamberlain, giving his opinion on the virtues of referen-dums and plebiscites. He said:
I have often wondered that we have never adopted the principle of the referendum as practised in Switzerland, and also in many parts of the United States of America. It is the only way in which the decision of great national questions can be separated from all the complicated issues of party government. At a general election the voter is influenced partly by his desire to see his own party in office, and partly by his views on a number of special questions, many of them purely local or even personal.
If, in the case of a new policy, not necessarily political, it were possible to eliminate all side issues, we might have a national verdict which all sections would accept, and which would be given without reference to the perennial struggle between the "Outs" and the "Ins" which is at present the chief occupation of political life.
I think those words are very appropriate at this time and I am very happy to have the opportunity of putting them on record in support of my arguments favouring the holding of a national referendum.
In conclusion, I hope this amendment will pass and that a plebiscite will be taken. If
Canadian Flag
this is not done, then I may say I, and some other members, are conducting plebiscites in our constituencies by mailing ballots to our constituents asking whether they favour the red ensign or the maple leaf. I have received some three to four thousand replies, and much to my regret the people voting to date are showing a preference for the red ensign on a ratio of about three to two.
My views on this amendment are not those of the majority of my party, but I hasten to add that we in the New Democratic party shall have a free vote in the house on this flag issue. I would like to see that free vote extended to all members in the house and to all people in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, much has been said in this house in connection with this debate and there is not too much I would want to add, except to add to some of the statements that were made by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz).
I too represent a constituency that is comprised of representatives of almost every ethnic group in this country. They are vitally interested in the issues which we choose to term the flag debate. The ethnic groups favour a distinctive Canadian flag with symbols, or a symbol which will bring national unity to Canada; because they have lived through the ravages of nationalism. The ethnic groups that came to Canada ran away from nationalism, and they are saying that Canada needs a nationality and not sectional nationalisms. In short, they hope that the founding races will find themselves.
The present resolution has been termed, perhaps, "Pearson's pennant" and it has been stated-as has just been stated by the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales)- that Pearson is trying to ram his flag down the throat of parliament and the Canadian people. The hon. member says that we have no right to do this, because we are a minority government. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that a minority government cannot railroad anything, because a minority government requires the support of members on the other side of this house in order to pass a resolution of this kind.
Hear, hear.
And I have no doubt that even members of the same party as the hon. member for Wellington South will be voting in favour of this resolution.

You haven't got a mandate.

Canadian Flag
If we were to give this resolution a subtitle, in my view we would not call it "Pearson's pennant" but rather "Pearson's penchant for peace".
Come out our way.

The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) stated that the ethnic groups respect the red ensign-and this is true. I must say that I was impressed by the colourful display we had on parliament hill with the red ensign. But we must in my view face the facts of life; and the facts of life are these, that in addition to the ethnic groups there are thousands of people in this country, perhaps millions, to whom the symbols of the red ensign represent defeat and humiliation.
Oh, oh.

I am not saying they are right, and I am not saying they are wrong; I am not taking issue with them. But the fact remains that there are thousands, or millions, of people in this country who consider that the symbols of the red ensign represent to them defeat, humiliation and domination.
What does Mr. St. Laurent say in that regard?

If they say that the symbols of the red ensign have certain connotations at one end of this country, and other connotations at other ends of the country; that in other sections of Canada the connotations are victory and domination-
No.

These are the facts of life. Some members have said that this resolution is appeasement to Quebec. May I point out one thing in this connection, namely that no member from Quebec, nor any editorial in any newspaper in Quebec, has set forth that it would like included in the new distinctive flag the fleur-de-lis or any other symbol of French Canada. French Canada wants a distinctive Canadian flag in order to be able to rally around some common denominator with the rest of Canada.
Hear, hear.
Have you ever heard of maple leaves out west?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have a few silly asses around the west.

I believe that we not only need a distinctive Canadian flag but we have to revise our history books in this country and

we have to stop fighting the battle of the plains of Abraham. Every successive generation keeps on fighting the battle of the plains of Abraham, and this is contributing to disunity in this country.
You are fighting it right now.

The history books should be factual, relating to what happened; but they should not dramatize and embellish the glories of a military commander. Mr. Speaker, I want to say just one more thing. The one issue upon which the entire house agreed-at least, in the time that I have been here-was the address to the Queen requesting the amendment to provide for survivors and disability benefits. In other words, every section of the house declared that it is a humiliating experience to have to go to another country in order to amend Canada's own constitution. If it is a humiliating experience-and this was agreed upon-to have to go to another country to amend our own constitution, is this not the greatest point in favour of having a distinctive Canadian flag? If the parliament of Great Britain to whom the amendment is addressed-I know that in practice they never refuse such amendments, but in theory they could refuse this amendment-refused this amendment there would be resentment throughout the length and breadth of this country. So, Mr. Speaker, I say in conclusion-
So you are still fighting that battle.
-let us stop talking in this country only about the things we are ready to die for. Let us talk about the things we are ready to live for in a great and united Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us today a very divisive issue in this resolution on the flag. It is a two-pronged resolution. It was intended as a one-vote resolution; but following the skills of those of other days in calling sinners to repentance, the resolution was split. Le Devoir carried an editorial on May 28 in which they accused the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of running with the hares and hunting with the hounds; or, in principle, of dividing Canada. You must ask yourself what madness prompted the Prime Minister to sponsor his own flag, revealed to others before it was even revealed to parliament, and then in the most dictatorial

manner he held our noses and poured the castor oil into our mouths without our having even the opportunity of freedom of choice. The Globe and Mail of June 16 had this to say about this mess:
A bitter wrangle between the defenders of the red ensign and the crusaders for a new maple leaf flag has raged across English speaking Canada and shows no sign of abating. In French speaking Canada there is dissatisfaction verging on disgust at Mr. Pearson's attempt to compromise by retaining the union jack as a flag to be flown on royal and commonwealth occasions. Whatever the outcome of these disputes now, it seems inevitable that large sections of the population will be left aggrieved and rebellious.
This is the unhappy state to which Mr. Pearson has reduced us, and it would be very natural if the opposition parties in the House of Commons sought to drive the lesson home as they debate the flag issue this week. They have every reason to be resentful of Mr. Pearson's tactics in threatening them with an election unless they accept the design he has chosen, and plenty of ammunition with which to discredit him.
This is the Prime Minister who a few years ago was a diplomat of some stature. He has made the flag issue a personal issue, regardless of all other pressing social and economic ills of this nation and regardless of other election promises which were far more important. Yet he presses the flag issue, even though it was not an election promise.
The Prime Minister stated on May 15 in this house that there were 38 pieces of legislation which must be passed before a summer recess. There was no mention of the flag whatever. What changed his mind, Mr. Speaker? He stirred up a lot of strife and emotion in parliament, but that does not matter much because we are paid to take it. But what about the emotions he has stirred up from the Atlantic to the Pacific across the land? If you do not think this is so, Mr. Speaker, just look at the editorials. Canada cannot afford this. I wonder whether the Prime Minister has become emotional on his own resolution when he says that this flag goes through without a free vote or we have an election. I wonder whether this is subtle closure, Mr. Speaker. He wants to bring in this flag with little or no regard for history or tradition.
I should like to put on record what the Midland Free Press has to say about this. This is a semi-weekly publication and has won many awards for its editorial page. In an editorial it says:
It is argued that the favourite among the new designs-the three red maple leaves on a white background and two blue bars at the hoist and the fly-will promote unity in a divided land.
We seriously question this contention and we believe a description of the symbolism of the red 20220-319
Canadian Flag
ensign and of the presently favoured design will illustrate the point.
The proposed new flag does not have much to offer in this regard. Its heraldic significance is shallow. The two blue bars represent the seas on our eastern and western coasts. The significance of the white background in the centre escapes us. The three red maple leaves are emblematic of a tree that grows in Canada, but they also are found in other lands as well.
Now let's look at the elements embodied in the Canadian red ensign.
In the upper left hand quadrant is a union of the crosses of St. George, St. Andrew and St. Patrick-patron saints respectively of England, Ireland and Scotland, it is true. The three ancient saints, however, were not nationals of the lands of the British Isles. They were chosen because of their great deeds and high ideals. St. George was a Macedonian, the patron saint of chivalry. St. Andrew, a Jew, was one of Christ's apostles who was martyred for his faith. St. Patrick was a missionary who spread among the Irish the civilization learned in France.
The peoples of Britain consist of a melting pot of Britons, Angles, Saxons, Piets, Scots, Romans and French. This part of our flag then links us with our ancient forefathers in the islands and mainlands of Europe.
Later on I shall make some reference to what a previous prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, said on this very point. The editorial continues:
It is said that a flag should be emblematic of its people. The shield from our coat of arms, contained in the fly of the ensign, would seem to do a pretty fair job in this regard. Emblazoned in the five parts of the shield are the three lions of England derived from the standard of William of Normandy; the lion rampant of Scotland; the harp of Ireland; the fleur-de-lis of France; and the three red maple leaves.
Both symbols-the union of crosses in the upper quadrant and the great shield-were not originally chosen for nationalistic reasons. They were selected because they symbolized "unity by agreement and the abandonment of narrow nationalism in favour of the brotherhood of man. The red background denotes a position of honour.
As a spokesman said, "The ensign is a flag with great depth of meaning capable of representing our complex idealism, our varied traditions and cultures, things a new design could not possibly match".
We agree. And if we exchange the ensign for a proposed new flag of much lesser consequence, it seems to us we will be swapping our birthright for a mess of pottage.
Do we really want, Mr. Speaker, to get rid of those symbols?
The Packet and Times for Monday, June 8 last, offers some sage advice; it is a paper whose editorials have been quoted all across Canada.
In his proposed design for a new Canadian flag, Mr. Pearson is attempting to avoid any conflict between English speaking and French speaking sections of the country, by omitting any British or French symbol whatever. In doing so, of course, he has produced a flag which represents nothing

Canadian Flag
whatever, and so has robbed the flag of the very function for which it is intended. For surely a flag has no meaning or value whatsoever, unless it be to represent heraldically the spirit of a nation, and so be an inspiration and source of pride to its citizens. A flag selected only because of its bland austerity and freedom from anything calculated to stir strong feeling, can hardly be valued for its inspirational qualities.
The whole issue of Canada's flag has blown up into ridiculous proportions, and has split still further a country already in need of all the unifying elements it can find. There is a dismaying tendency to value the symbol at the expense of the reality; it is Canada that is truly important, not the design of the flag it chooses to fly. In the bitter bickering over that design, some sense of proportion must be maintained. It is utter folly to speak, as some have done, of breaking up confederation if this or that design is not chosen.
Yet once the relative importance of the issue has been established, it is quite right that something should be said about the value of retaining in the national flag the symbols of this country's origins. The two great facts of our national existence are, first, our British heritage, which gave us our language, our laws, our form of government and indeed, all the principles and values which guide our way of life; and second, the empire of new France which was joined with British North America in full and equal partnership. Surely any flag purporting to represent this country must reflect this dual origin of all the institutions and outlooks which are uniquely Canadian, and which impart a distinctly Canadian character to people and nation. It is the measure of the total inadequacy of Mr. Pearson's proposed flag that its symbolism reflects not a trace of this rich and unique national heritage.
The objection to the existing Canadian flag, based on the red ensign, is that it does not sufficiently indicate the French partnership in this great nation. Surely this is capable of easy remedy, perhaps by the replacement of the existing Canadian coat of arms in the fly by large fleur-de-lis, singly or in a group, to share pride of place with the union jack on the traditional red background. Something of the kind could certainly be evolved which would be both heraldically correct and visually attractive, as well as truly indicative of this country's national origins.
A real Canadian ensign, so evolved, would perpetuate both a traditional design under which this country has grown and prospered and under which its troops have fought in two world wars, and reflect the long history of a unique racial partnership. Such origins are to be perpetuated proudly, not buried in the bland anonymity of a piece of white bunting. A flag is intended to stir emotion, not dampen it. Only an amended red ensign can truly reflect this nation's pride in its past and its aspirations for the future.
This sets out some compelling reasons why symbols of the past should be retained. I intend now to quote one of the great prime ministers of this land, a man who was in power longer than any other prime minister in the British commonwealth, Mr. Mackenzie King. This is what he said:
The new Canadian flag should certainly contain the union jack. It would be unthinkable to have a
[Mr. Rynard.l
flag for this dominion which did not contain the union jack.
This was said by Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King in a statement to the Canadian Legion in 1945. I also wish to quote what was said by prime minister Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent in the House of Commons in 1949. He said this:
The union jack is a symbol which represents much that is best in the heritage of all those who derive their tradition and their culture from western Europe.
I wish to say that part of my family ties are with western Europe. The quotation goes on:
The crosses that are part of the union jack represent much of what we in Canada, from whatever race we spring, all honour as precious and good in our heritage...I do not believe that any of us in this country regard the union jack as being a symbol of conquest or subjugation. It is under the union jack that the institutions of this Canadian nation have grown and developed and have brought us to the point where now the dominion is and has been an autonomous state subject in no phase of its domestic or its external affairs to any authority other than this Canadian parliament.
I should like to comment on a reference which was made by one of the previous speakers to the British North America Act. Let me say that the British North America Act was drawn up by Canadians, not by English people. It was drawn up at Charlottetown and in Quebec.
I have talked to several Canadians of French origin from Quebec and they have told me the flag is a waning issue for them. It is not very important any more. They said: We have our own flag, the fleur-de-lis; we could not care less about the flag; what is important is control over our own economy and we shall not brook any more interference from Ottawa on this point. This is what I gather after talking to important French speaking Canadians in the city of Montreal. This would imply that the question of the flag is not the big issue in Quebec we have been led to believe it is. Certainly, in my riding, of those who have written to me- and I have received more than 500 letters- over 90 per cent were in favour of the red ensign and the rest were divided in their opinions.
I believe a perusal of history would indicate a desire to retain symbols of the past in any new flag we might choose. When I see the three lions on the flag, I immediately think of William the Conqueror coming from Normandy, and I believe 90 per cent of all the people who come to this land, to the

province of Quebec, are of Norman stock. That is their proud heritage. It was William the Conqueror who came to the throne of England after defeating Harold at the battle of Hastings. Let me remind the house that the parliament of England and the ruling class of that country used the French language for 300 years. The first income tax bill was written by William the Conqueror. The first census was taken by William the Conqueror, and I am proud that a man coming from Europe did that. It showed administrative ability, and I am also proud of the fact that it was by one of this line of Norman kings that the first great charter, the cornerstone of British democracy, was written. I refer to Magna Carta commonly known as the great charter. We honour that and we respect it, no matter what our country of origin, because it is a cornerstone of parliamentary democracy. It was a Norman king who was forced to sign that charter. It was drawn up by the Norman barons at Runny-mede and it became the father, or the mother, or whatever you like of the great bill of rights which gave this country freedom of choice, freedom of election, freedom of religion and freedom of assembly.
Over those 300 years of history the English language became a melting pot of the Norman and the English tongues and out of that evolved the English language which is spoken today by the strongest and greatest nation in the world, just south of us. I am proud of that, Mr. Speaker. I am proud of the part the Normans played and I am proud of the fact that a great part of the English people belong to that Norman stock. Surely those of us who are of that stock do not want to throw it out the window or sell it for a colourless piece of cloth which does not mean anything to us.
In the course of history a few hundred years later a great event took place on the plains of Abraham. I am always proud when I read about it because many of the soldiers who fought there were soldiers from this melting pot of English, Norman and Scotch. There were also Norman soldiers under Montcalm. I read those pages of history and I am proud to learn that Montcalm was a man who loved his homeland and who, in his letters to his wife and daughters, said he hoped he would soon be able to join them back home. He was a home loving man and he was a great soldier of high moral principles. I am also proud to know that Wolfe wrote home regularly to his mother and that the night before the battle of the plains of Abraham, as they 20220-319i
Canadian Flag
floated down the St. Lawrence, he pulled a copy of Gray's Elegy from his pocket and read it. When he had read it, he said: Fellow officers, I would rather have written that than capture Quebec tomorrow. Both these two great generals were killed on the plains of Abraham and I want to say that out of their ashes, out of the things they gave to Canada, has arisen a mighty nation of which we are all proud. We are proud of the part each of them played; we are proud of them. We are proud of the pages they have given to history.
I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that poor indeed will be the lot in tradition of the young people of this country when those pages are removed from their history books. Do we really want to give up the symbols of the past? As I go through the pages of history and come to the American revolution I think of the French, and how they stood nobly by with their brothers. Yes, the English were Normans, do not forget it; they were a mixture of Normans, Piets, Scots, and so forth. They stood nobly by; they were the staunchest of people, saying: We do not want any part of the American republic; we want to maintain our loyalty to the crown that will protect our rights and that gave us the Quebec Act.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, these same people fought alongside us in the first great war. Who make these differences? Is it the politicians?
I wonder. It is not the people, because they fought alongside us in the first great war.
I think also of the present Governor General of this country who fought in that war and was seriously injured. I come to the next great war and I think of another French Canadian, the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod of the other place, who was severely wounded. We have fought for the same causes and the same principles over the years.
What is wrong, Mr. Speaker? Do we want to change the flag? Do we want to retain our symbols? My feeling is that this country has done a tremendous task and nothing should be done now to divide the country. When the Prime Minister takes it upon himself to shove down the throats of members of parliament a flag which he says represents all that is good in Canada but which leaves out all our past history, then I think we would be derelict in our duty if we did not fight to the last ditch to retain those principles that have made Canada the great nation it is, and a part of any new flag.
Is there any good reason for shoving the flag through at the expense of much more

Canadian Flag
important legislation left in mothballs, legislation that this country is crying for and needs? Does the Prime Minister not realize that he in effect is using a subtle form of blackmail or closure through the threat of an election? Or is there a feeling of divine right? This view was more or less expressed the other day by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) when she said it did not matter much what your constituents thought, that you should vote regardless of their wishes. I am one of those who have always felt that the people of one's riding are those who decide how a member should vote, because they elect the member as their representative.
Why is the flag issue the supreme issue before the house? Will it change the economy of Canada one whit? Will it improve the lot of any Canadian home the day after it is adopted? Will it put one more dollar in the pockets of the taxpayers? Will it improve the security of even one Canadian? As one writer noted, the Prime Minister may imagine that he is bold and daring but his armour is completely that of foolhardiness. On May 15 last the Prime Minister outlined 38 pieces of government legislation which he said must be completed before a summer recess and, as I said, the flag issue was not among them. Why the haste? Is it to conceal something? Is it to get off the hook on more important issues? I suggest that the most important issue confronting Canada today is automation and employment. If we do not solve this problem hundreds of thousands of young Canadians will be walking the streets in a few years.
The Prime Minister knows he is in trouble because of his two flag stand. Most people do not want a two flag nation. Passions are being roused across the country. I am one of those who try to carry out the wishes of my constituents as far as possible. Therefore 1 think the people of Canada should be allowed to express their opinion.
I want to remind the Prime Minister that he is the head of a minority government. Only 42 per cent of the people of Canada supported his minority government. If the Prime Minister will not let the people of Canada decide this referendum, will he consider setting up a dominion-provincial conference, provide the delegates with the assistance of historians and heraldic experts, and let them do the job? Then we will have a flag picked democratically and, above all, we will have one flag instead of ten. We will have a flag representative of Canada, not of only two provinces.
[Mr. Rvnard.l
The Prime Minister has a unique challenge today. I say to him: Take off this foolhardy armour; get rid of this bold and daring approach and go back to the approach of Sir John A. Macdonald, William Lyon Mackenzie King-St. Laurent, Cartier, Lafontaine, Baldwin and others. Let him cease to be a despot, a dictator with a minority government. Let him again restore democratic principles to this parliament and respect the wishes of the peoples who make up the mosaic that is Canada, who are proud of Canada, proud of our past, proud of our history and do not want to trade these symbols for a mess of potage.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to make it quite clear that I am going to vote for both parts of the resolution.
I am going to vote for two flags. I am going to vote for a distinctive Canadian flag and I am going to vote for the union jack.
I do not make any apologies for the fact that I intend to vote for two flags. I think that with the passage of time Canadians will be indicating loyalty to a number of flags. Foremost among these flags, at least in the minds of those who are international in their outlook, will be the flag of the United Nations. They will be looking also to the flag which denotes our connection with the commonwealth family of nations, the union jack, which is found in the second part of the main resolution presented to the house several weeks ago. They will be looking to a distinctive national flag for Canada, the maple leaf flag, the flag that will be passed during the current session of parliament.
There will also be provincial flags across this country. There are several in existence at the moment. There is one in Newfoundland, the union jack. There is one in Quebec, which most of us have seen flying. It is composed of a white cross on a pale blue background with four white fleur de lis, one in each corner. There is a flag in one of our other rather nationalistic provinces, the province of British Columbia. The flag prominently displays the union jack. There is also a flag in Nova Scotia. In heraldic terms at least this flag dates back to the early 1600's. It is essentially the cross of St. Andrew with a lion rampant representing Scotland on the centre of the flag.
These four categories of flags at least will be regarded as important by Canadians. I repeat that those who are internationally minded will tend to look more to the flag of the United Nations and to the union jack.

Those who are more provincially minded will tend to look to our provincial flags, club emblems and so on. But there will be more than one flag prominently displayed across this nation.
A flag is used as a banner to rally people together, to rally forces, to focus the interest and attention of the populace at large. It is used to identify groups, provinces, nations and peoples. It is also used to celebrate historic events and highlight recent accomplishments. These are the various purposes of flags, banners and coats of arms of different kinds. But these are merely the symbols. Underlying them are the basic ideas, the basic concepts for which a flag or coat of arms stands.
These concepts, these ideas are what is really important. They are the essence of our modern democracy and of any substantial crusade to get things done. The union jack means a great deal to many people. It means a great deal to members, like me, who come from British Columbia. To me and to many other British Columbians it signifies courage, confidence; it indicates compassion and it also is a symbol of Christianity and Christian ideals. I am certain that we will continue to fly it, that is the union jack, because of the basic ideas which it symbolizes, because of the history and tradition in which those various ideas have been displayed.
Now, we need a national flag as a means of identification of Canadians, particularly Canadians abroad. It would be particularly useful at this moment if the Canadian forces on Cyprus had a distinctive Canadian flag because they could be identified, not as forces from the United Kingdom, not as forces from other commonwealth countries, but specifically from Canada. Canada is thought by many countries to be unbiased, lacking in territorial ambitions, and so on. For these reasons I think it is important that our forces have this distinguishing mark.
I should like briefly to make reference to the concept of nationhood, of nationality. In this connection I should like to quote from the first chapter of a book which has recently been published, entitled, "The New Nationality". The author is Frank H. Underhill, and he states in this book-and I think interestingly-
A nation is a body of men who have done great things together in the past and who hope to do great things together in the future. What makes them into a nation is not necessarily community of race, language and religion, though these are powerful forces when they are present; it is their common history and traditions, their experience of living together, their having done great things
Canadian Flag
together in the past, and their determination to continue doing great things together in the future.
Now, Canadians in their history have not seen many sharp and dramatic changes. Most of the changes which have taken place in our great country have been gradual. I should like briefly to run over and contrast them with the histories of other countries. Throughout history, many of the great nations of the world have been in conflict when they were born, and they grew to maturity beset by danger and tribulation. Out of these circumstances rose strong and fervent feelings of patriotism and nationalism, fanned by difficulty and nurtured by opposition.
Under such circumstances, a feeling of national identity came quickly to the fore. National heroes were made. They were men who fought or died or faced prison or exile for the new nation. Great landmarks in the form of battles won or lost were stamped on the national consciousness. To these people, the Bismarcks, the Cavours, the Simon Bolivars, the Gandhis, the de Valeras, and to these historic events, new citizens could look for inspiration and for a spirit of dedication.
A great example of this of course is in our neighbour to the south. Born in desperate revolution, nurtured in the crucible of the civil war, the United States quickly established its national heroes such as George Washington, Jefferson, Hamilton, Lee and others; its historic landmarks; its character and identity. Its first citizens gained their independence in blood and toil, and the facts of history were starkly etched for future generations to see.
We in Canada do not have the advantage, if one may call it an advantage, or such a violent and spectacular birth. We came to nationhood through negotiation and consent. We reached independence without forfeiting the connection with our ancient motherland. We achieved maturity without hostility and identity without violence.
All this has left its mark on our national character. Most Canadians tend to be moderate in their decisions, unexcitable in their attitudes, slow to anger and not prone to extreme positions. So it is in this matter of national symbols. I do not believe that as Canadians we should regret the fact that we have to spend a few weeks of parliament's time to arrive at a national flag, a national symbol, when by contrast we look at the wars, the revolutions, the extreme emergencies out of which other nations were born,

Canadian Flag
and as a result of which they established their own symbols.
I should like briefly to run over the reasons for choosing the colours in the distinctive Canadian flag, the colours red, white and blue. There are many historical reasons for choosing this grouping of colours. The first white men to set foot on North America, historians now tell us, were the Vikings. Essentially a northern, or a Norman people, from whom both our French speaking and English speaking ethnic groups are largely derived, these adventurers set foot on North America around the year 1,000. Back in those days, a flag of the type that we now know did not exist. One of the identifying marks was the sail-the colours of the sails of the ships in those days. The colours of the sails of the Viking ships were red stripes on a white background. The red and white were established there. The black raven of these northern people also was displayed on some of these ships, but the colours predominantly were red and white.
Cabot touched Cape Breton about 500 years later, in 1493. The flag he flew was the cross of St. George, red and white. In 1524, some years later, Jacques Cartier first arrived in Canada. Jacques Cartier flew the flag of France. Down through two centuries after that, variations of the flag of France appeared and were flown in what is now eastern Canada. They were substantially the fleur-de-lis and various groupings of the fleur-de-lis on several backgrounds, red, white and blue. Again therefore the red, white and blue colours appeared in our background.
Henry Hudson flew the first union jack that was shown in Canada in Hudson bay in the year 1610, a few years after the first union jack was struck. The union jack then was a combination of the cross of St. George and the cross of St. Andrew, red, white and blue. The union jack was again established on Canadian territory in Nova Scotia in the early years prior to the battle of the plains of Abraham. The union jack was raised on the plains of Abraham in 1759. It included the cross of St. Patrick after 1800 and it was the official flag of Canada down to the early 1920's, although a variation of the red ensign was flown by our merchant marine and occasionally from buildings both inside and outside of Canada.
In 1921, Canada's official coat of arms was struck. It was the result of careful deliberation and a careful review of heraldry. This coat of arms was introduced and confirmed

by a Conservative government. It bears the historic emblems of England, Ireland, Scotland and France in the top part of the shield. Incidentally, the top part of the shield denotes the historic background of the nation or an individual. If one hires an expert in heraldry to go into his family background, he will find the history of his family is on the top part of the shield and the individual himself, the present, is on the bottom part of the shield. On the bottom part of the shield as introduced, formalized and finally adopted by Canada in 1921 are three red maple leaves conjoined on a single stem on a white background.
This was the first time on which the three red maple leaves on a white background were officially proclaimed. This is now Canada's official coat of arms and has been for the past 40 and more years. There was a cabinet minute passed in 1957 which further clarified the red leaves on a white background. Many red ensigns flying today still show green leaves, but this is not true to the legislation of the early twenties and the cabinet minute of 1957.
In 1963, in order to clarify matters further, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) asked a question of the previous government. He asked, "What are Canada's national colours?" and the answer came back, red on white. He also asked, "What is Canada's national symbol?" and the answer came back, "Three red maple leaves on a white background." Therefore during the life of the previous administration this was recognized officially, first confirmed and then officially recognized in answer to questions posed by the opposition, that our national colours are red on white and the official emblem of Canada is three red maple leaves conjoined on a single stem on a white background.
I would like to refer briefly to the form of the flag, but before doing so I shall make a reference to Canada's colours at the Olympic games. They have always been red on white, red maple leaves on a white background. Similar colour combinations have been shown at our national exhibitions, beginning back in 1905 at Turin, Italy; so that we have a long history of red maple leaves on a white background as part of our Canadian tradition.
As to the matter of form, there are various requirements of a distinctive emblem. These are that it should be easily recognizeable, that it should not be like the emblem of any other country. It should be visible at a considerable distance, as well as close up to those

who are looking for its designation. It should also be symbolic of the country and characteristic of the nation.
These requirements are not met by many flags; hence those flags are not truly distinctive. I should like to indicate some flags of this type, flags of the red ensign type, and this information I obtained from the parliamentary library. They appear on a card headed "Flags of the Commonwealth," and I should like to describe these flags. There is, of course, most prominently the union jack, and under it the flags of Canada, Australia, New Zealand and many other countries. The flag that is typical of the colonies resembles the flags of Australia and New Zealand. There is the union jack up in the canton, next to the pole, and the distinguishing mark is on the blue or red background. The blue background, or blue peter as it is sometimes called, is more common in the case of colonies, but there are variations.
On the chart in front of me I see 33 different territories or colonies whose unique badges appear in the fly, in the same fashion or manner as the now official Canadian coats of arms appears in the fly of the Canadian red ensign, and for the record I would like to read out what these are. Their flags resemble the red ensign of Canada, with the union jack up in the corner, and the shield or circle down in the opposite corner, and they include Aden colony, Antigua, Barbados, Bahamas, Bermuda, British Guiana, British Honduras, British Solomon Islands, British Virgin Islands, the Caymen islands, Dominica, The Falkland islands, the federation of Rhodesia and Nyasal-and, Fiji, Gambia, Gibraltar, Gilbert and Elice Islands, Grenada, Hong Kong, Kenya, Mauritius, Montsarrat, North Borneo, Northern Rhodesia, Nyasaland, St. Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla, St. Helena, St. Lucia, St. Vincent, Sarawak, Seychelles, Southern Rhodesia, Turks and Caicos Islands. Those are flags of various colonies and other territories around the world which are of the ensign type.
I should also like to put on the record a quotation taken from "Flags of the World", edited by Gresham Carr and published in London in 1956, and the remarks in it bear more particularly on the type of red ensign flown by the British merchant marine around the world:
Some commonwealth merchant vessels-of Canada, the commonwealth of Australia, New Zealand, Cyprus, Somaliland, Western Samoa and Tanganyika territory, and of the British North Borneo Company-may, by admiralty warrant, wear the red ensign with the badge of the dominion, state, protectorate, or trust territory in the fly, but other
Canadian Flag
colonial merchant vessels shall wear the red ensign free from any badge or distinctive mark.
Any colonial merchant vessel may, however, wear a distinguishing flag with the badge of the colony thereon, in addition to the red ensign, provided that such a flag does not infringe the provisions of the merchants shipping act of 1894.
Again, still quoting,
A few yacht clubs have permission to wear the red ensign defaced-
That is a proper term
-by the badge of the club.
There are, in addition, numerous companies which over the centuries have been given permission-the Hudson's Bay Company is one of them-to put their own identification on the fly of a red ensign type flag, and hence around the world you have numerous territories, groups, other organizations and many private corporations which have official permission to fly a flag which at more than a few hundred yards distance cannot be distinguished from the Canadian red ensign.
I am reasonably certain that the vast majority of Canadians could not tell us what is on the shield of Canada, and hence what is on the badge of the Canadian red ensign. Indeed I would be surprised if the majority of members of parliament could quickly reel off what is on this distinctive badge in the fly of the red ensign at the present time. Therefore clearly the Canadian red ensign, which is officially adopted as our flag pending action by parliament, is not a unique emblem or flag for use in international gatherings such as at the United Nations.
Continuing on the form of the flag, the history of the three maple leaves dates back more than a century. There were a number of organizations which adopted the maple leaf as their symbol prior to 1867.
In 1860 a significant incident occurred when the then Prince of Wales visited Toronto. It was planned that all native Canadians would join in a procession, wearing the maple leaf as an emblem of the land of their birth. The Toronto Globe of that time tells us that they would therefore-
-be known to the world as such and as loyal subjects to Her Majesty.
It also expressed the hope that the-
*-first public act of His Royal Highness, after presenting its banners to the Royal Canadian Regiment, would doubtless be that of sanctioning the adoption of the maple leaf as our national emblem.
The establishment of the coats of arms of Ontario and Quebec in 1868, immediately after confederation, is also of significance because three maple leaves conjoined on a single stem appear at the base of both of these coats of

Canadian Flag
arms. The coat of arms of Ontario includes three gold maple leaves on a green background. Incidentally, these maple leaves appear much larger than on the coat of arms of Quebec, because in the case of Quebec the top part, the historical part, of the shield includes both three fleur-de-lis on a blue background and the lions passant, representing the English ethnic stock of Quebec. The Quebec shield has at the base three green maple leaves on a gold background.
In heraldry the top colours, the most distinctive colours, are rated as follows; red, white, blue, and so on down to the less easily distinguishable colours. It is significant that neither red, white nor blue were used in the coats of arms of Ontario or Quebec at that time, in 1868. So presumably red on white or white on red was reserved for the nation, as they take precedence in terms of distinctiveness and certainly in terms of heraldic value. In 1921, of course, the heralds of that day were able to take advantage of the more distinctive colours, red on white, and confirmed the three maple leaves on a white background as the Canadian portion of our official coat of arms.
From 1868 onward many military medals were struck and most, if not all, of them have shown maple leaves, frequently three maple leaves on a single stem on the reverse side of the medal. "The maple leaf forever" was written in the late 1860's by Alexander Muir. In 1939 the battle flag of the first Canadian division was struck. This flag has been described by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson); it contains three maple leaves prominently displayed on a red ensign-type flag and also shows three gold fleur-de-lis on a blue background. The service pin that veterans wore at the end of world war II is substantially a shield topped by a crown. It has a white background displaying three red maple leaves conjoined on a single stem.
In 1946 a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate sat for some considerable period of time and considered over 2,000 different designs for a Canadian flag. By far and away the most popular design contained one or more maple leaves. If that was any indication of the preference of Canadians of that day, the maple leaf was certainly at the top of the list.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Plus the jack in the corner. What was the choice of the committee?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Since then there have been various insignia and symbols adopted by our armed forces. During world war II, as

many hon. members will remember, the air force insignia was the rondel, the circles red, white and blue; but instead of the red circular core which appears in the Royal Air Force rondel, we had a red maple leaf. We now have a red maple leaf on the funnels of our destroyers and other naval vessels. We have maple leaves appearing as the distinguishing mark on our military vehicles in the army, and we now have on the official cars drawing up before the House of Commons three maple leaves prominently displayed as the distinguishing mark of Canadian sovereignty.
The Queen's personal flag, struck in 1962, contains on the top part, indicating our ethnic background again, the three lions passant of England, the lion rampant of Scotland, the three gold fleur-de-lis on a blue background, of royal France, and the harp of Ireland; but in the bottom half you have three maple leaves conjoined on a single stem, indicating the Canada of today and tomorrow, and printed on top of all this is "E.R.", "Elizabeth, Regina".
In concluding this portion of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to colour and design. Certainly one of the group of seven great Canadian artists, Mr. A. Y. Jackson, seems to agree that three red maple leaves on a white background is appropriate. Remarks to this effect have appeared in the newspapers recently and I will merely quote from the Montreal Star of June 28. He is speaking about a design which he had prepared some three years ago and which, incidentally, bears a striking resemblance to the present proposed design, the design described in the first part of the resolution. Mr. Jackson is quoted as saying:
"We had to decide either on an emblem or an abstract design such as a tricolour-
This is Mr. A. Y. Jackson speaking recently when he was interviewed by the press:
-and there's so many of those-
He is referring to abstract designs:
-it's hard to get a distinctive flag. We have no animal-the heaver looks like a rat-and so the maple leaf seems best.
"Having decided that, the government should have called for suggestions-
I will skip the rest of that paragraph. Then he said:
"You have to think how a flag will look through a telescope from three or four miles away".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Who owns a telescope?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
He continues:
"One maple leaf, from that distance, might look like a circle or something and the flag would not

be distinctive. The three leaves would make it distinctive".
So this is the view of A. Y. Jackson.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Get out your telescope.
It looks like the Russian merchant flag.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to go back just for a moment to the matter of several flags. I mentioned the United Nations flag, the union jack which is essentially the commonwealth flag, our own distinctive national flag and the provincial flags. I am certain that more provinces will be striking flags with the passage of time. I think some, acting soon perhaps, will be inclined to adopt a variation of the red ensign. This may not be, heraldically, correct, but they could remove the Canadian coat of arms and add the provincial coat of arms; or, for example, in the case of Ontario you could have an ensign type flag with the cross of St. George next to the pole, in the upper left-hand corner, and the three gold maple leaves in the opposite corner, on the fly, the background being green. This would be in conformity with the coat of arms of Ontario and heraldically correct. Similar flags could be struck in other provinces, with the cross of St. George or the union jack frequently appearing next to the pole.
I would like to remark that all the parties represented in this House of Commons have at one time or another passed resolutions favouring a distinctive Canadian flag. I stressed earlier that a distinctive Canadian flag is not an ensign type flag-it is certainly not a red ensign type flag. I might also have added that an ensign type flag is rated below flags like the union jack. In other words, the union jack in an ensign is in the superior position, and hence flags with derivatives of the three maple leaves, for example, would have three maple leaves in the corner and variations down below on the remaining three quarters of the flag.
All parties in this house have passed resolutions at the grassroots level favouring a distinctive Canadian flag; hence they have a responsibility to face up to this issue.
Across the country we have a variety of opinion and I think most members have received a great deal of mail on this subject. I would like briefly to break down the mail which I have received in order to give an impression of the popular response, the popular participation, in this matter.
There is a middle group of people who, I suggest, may encompass three quarters of the 20220-320
Canadian Flag
population, perhaps 80 per cent or more. This middle group includes many English speaking Canadians. They would like us to have a distinctive flag, a flag which would not be confused with the flag of any other country in, for example, a United Nations ceremony. Many of these people are of British origin, who are what one might say British to the core, but they are Canadians first. Many English speaking Canadians with a sentimental attachment to the union jack or red ensign have a kindly understanding of the French speaking Canadians who would have Canada's flag distinctive and purely Canadian. Many a French speaking Canadian wishes a purely Canadian flag but wants this without any venom or disrespect to the Englishspeaking portion of our great Canadian community. These people in my belief make up the vast majority of Canadians; I would put the figure as high as 80 per cent.
There are two other groups, distinct minorities. One has certainly earned its right to speak up for a flag, and let no one belittle its right. It includes many of the men and women who are prominent in organizations such as the Canadian Legion and the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire. I think our job is to convince them that it was freedom, democracy and true British justice they were fighting for, not just for a flag. I think most of them on second thought will agree with this. They might account for 10 per cent of the Canadian public, but I doubt it.
Finally there is a small group of people who are essentially malcontents-separatists and the like. There are some French speaking Canadians who want no part of a Canadian flag which bears the union jack. They are not necessarily venomous but perhaps blind to a large part of our past.
There is a similar group of people in English speaking Canada. Its members are not very numerous but they feel very strongly that English speaking Canadians have the right, because of their majority, to dictate to the rest of the country. They are not thinking in family terms. They are not thinking of our neighbours or of relatives of other tongues as Canadians. They are thinking purely in a dogmatic fashion which knows no respect to the ideals and traditions which I believe are embodied in the union jack. Together these two small groups, this minority, if you like, of malcontents, may account for 2 or 3 per cent of the population of Canada. Their prejudices I think should be disregarded.

Canadian Flag
In view of this breakdown, Mr. Speaker, I can see little point in a national referendum. A national referendum would be overwhelmingly in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag. But what happens if we had a referendum? We have had two referendums in the history of Canada, and both appeals to the people over the heads of members of parliament have been frustrated because parliament, after the referendum results were in, refused to act and did not legislate. Hence the referendums in those two cases, in 1898 and in 1942, were purposeless.
Should we have a referendum, and the result be inconclusive? I doubt it. I think we would have a conclusive result. Hence a referendum is purposeless.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: It saves us from dictation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Once the results of the referendum were in, assuming one were held, and parliament had acted, then I think we would have to petition the Queen to ask other countries not to use the red ensign-type flag. Otherwise we would not have a distinctive Canadian flag flying throughout the world. We would also have to petition that the merchant marine of the United Kingdom not fly the red ensign. I think our recent experience in having to refer the social security legislation in the form of an amendment to the British North America Act to Westminster is sufficient indication of the difficulties involved and its complications. As a sovereign nation we should no longer have to go through this procedure, and in order to establish a distinctive Canadian flag this would resemble the ridiculous. I have merely given this example, Mr. Speaker, in order to illustrate how difficult it would be to establish a red ensign-type flag as a distinctive national flag.

It is the ideas behind the flag which are important-the ideas of liberty and opportunity. This is the imaginative concept, the type of ideas, which can lift up Canadians, lift up their eyes and stimulate their imagination. It will help to unify this country, I am convinced. instead of taking away from our emblems or destroying them. I believe Canadians of the future will fly United Nations flags, will prominently fly the union jack, they will fly our new national flag, provincial flags-

Mr. Speaker, no subject comes home more closely to the heart of a people or appeals more clearly to the intelligence of its citizens than the flag-its traditions, its history, its "prestige", its many and vital meanings.
On taking part in this debate I do so fully realizing that this past few days on the radio and in the papers, certain people have suggested that debating this issue is hopeless and wasting the time of the house. Sir, I suggest to you that no one knows this better than the Prime Minister himself and those who are helping to engineer and steer the passage of this resolution through the house.
I do not believe there has ever been an issue which has been so cleverly conceived by a government, knowing that it can win the vote in the house with certain members of the opposition playing a most important role and acting in co-operation with the government. The suggestion that parliament should make the decision is only another concealment, because these same proponents of the new flag know full well, if they let the people of Canada vote on this issue, what the result will be, and that they with their lust for power and dictatorship will receive in full measure the decision of the people.
Some days ago, the Prime Minister stated that only on two previous occasions had a plebiscite been carried out in Canada, once in 1898, on prohibition, and again in 1942, on conscription. I say, sir, that this, too, would be a plebiscite on prohibition brought on by a government drunk with power and certainly increasingly prone to dictatorship.
Also, when the Prime Minister introduced this resolution he stated that the red ensign was not acknowledged until the second world war; again, apparently the Prime Minister misinformed the house. I would like to read an extract from the Peterborough Examiner on this point; it has been referred to already by the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) but I know there are some hon. members here in 20220-320J

the house today who were not present at the time he read it. It states:
In 1900 the Fenian raid medal was struck carrying the red ensign. This was the first Canadian military decoration to be presented veterans by the government of Canada.

It is evident he could not have heard the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood) last night when he spoke about certain other flags. Gresham Carr which I obtained from the parliamentary library. On turning to page 190 reference is made to the flags of the Soviet union.
