I suggest that this proposed flag of the Prime Minister is not distinctive from any other flag. We want to destroy our red ensign because it is the symbol of the British merchant marine and replace it with a flag with the white background, the blue trim and the red of the Soviet union.
The nub of the flag controversy seems to be the use of the union jack. Those who object to the prominence of the union jack do so because they feel it denotes subordination to a sovereign power other than Canada. I feel however that the union jack is much more than a flag of England or the United Kingdom. The truth is that it never was the flag of England alone. It incorporates what used to be England's standard, but it is made up of various traditions. Long ago, from Normandy, France, we brought the crusaders' emblem, the cross of St. George-England's patron saint-and it became the banner of the kingdom centuries later. Scotland and England were united under the Stuarts. Thus, the cross of St. Andrew

Scotland's patron saint -was linked to the standard of St. George, and as a result of a flag with two crosses came to represent the United Kingdom. It was this flag which flew over Quebec when the treaty of Paris was signed in 1763, and when the Quebec Act was passed. Years after, in 1807, as a matter of fact, when Ireland joined the union, the cross of Ireland's patron saint-St. Patrick-was added.
Thus the union jack appeared. It was never the banner of a single country. From the be-

Canadian Flag
ginning it stood tor "united nations". It was the flag of the United Kingdom and Ireland. With the expansion ot the British empire went the union jack, carrying in its wake civilization and Christianity. It represents countless blessings to humanity.
The union jack is the symbol of our freedom maintained. It tells us of our explorers, reformers, and colonizers sailing the oceans of the world to bring Christian civilization, justice and liberties, the pioneering instinct, the benefits of science and a great literature, to the far flung corners of the earth.
French Canada, under the shield of the crown, was never held subject or kept servile, but carried on in the enjoyment of her ancient faith, customs, and language, and received its Magna Carta in the Quebec Act; and we have prospered and flourished into nationhood with the statute of Westminster in 1931.
Today the union jack speaks to us and our world neighbours of the commonwealth in a much broader way. It is the emblem of a free family of nations in which Canada is regarded as the mature daughter. What an example this family gives to the rest of humanity, and particularly to the United Nations organization. Do hon. members recall the conference of the commonwealth prime ministers in London at the coronation-a conference which had no treaty shackles, no rigid agenda, and no cold formality? It was a family gathering. Around that conference table sat a group of spokesmen for hundreds of millions of people of all races, colours, and creeds, drawn together by an act of faith and by the mysticism of the crown.
With Canada's active and predominant role in that commonwealth conference, and in world councils, there is no evidence that her right or power has been subordinated to any other sovereign power. Yet there is a segment of our population who apparently have an inferiority complex and believe themselves to be a servile race held in subjugation by another sovereign power, and are vassals. In the strange aberrations of their minds, they imagine that by the removal of the union jack from our flag they will be released from a mythical yoke.
One does not have to be of British origin or British in outlook to appreciate the British institutions of freedom. Distinction is something that is earned; culture is something that time creates. You do not build a culture trying to destroy another one or by trying to deny that another one exists. You give free vent to all worth-while cultural influences. We are what we are today because of

these ideals and institutions, which have given us both distinction and culture.
It is the spirit we want, something we feel yet cannot touch. We have ridden through nights of a thousand perils and the spirit is still strong within us. The symbolism of the union jack is spiritual. It is something above and which should be above all politics. It would be a pity if there were no nation on this continent to carry the union jack on into the future and, with strength and vitality, to give it the prominence it so justly deserves.
In searching for a distinctive national flag for Canada there is much to suggest that we have such a flag in the red ensign, which has become recognized as a symbol of Canadian autonomy within the British commonwealth of nations. Flags, as symbols of the deepest emotions of a nation, arise from the hearts of the people and not from formal edicts of a parliamentary body. Certainly our Canadian way of life, rooted and grounded in the British parliamentary institutions, can be symbolized in no better way than by a flag which is rich in spiritual content and features prominently that which only flags in the British commonwealth possess, the Christian concept. The cross of St. George, the cross of St. Andrew and the cross of St. Patrick are symbols of our redemption. This flag, with the three crosses of Christianity flying on the four winds of the Canadian heavens, will wave us forward along that difficult path to the universal communion of the brotherhood of man. It is emblematic of the source from whence our greatness came.

In my own opinion, Mr. Speaker, the true number of names in favour of the red ensign has not been given to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or I am certain he would not have proceeded with this resolution. Just the other day, sir, I attended the funeral of a veteran of world war II. On this soldier's casket rested the red ensign, the flag that he lived for and the flag that he died for. After the funeral, I was talking to his three sons, two living in Toronto and one in my own riding. They remarked that throughout their lives they and their parents had always been supporters of the Liberal party. However, if Mr. Pearson

forced this flag issue, never again would they cast a Liberal vote.
I say to the people of Canada that the Prime Minister has betrayed the boys with whom he fought. He has betrayed the 100,000 Canadians who gave their lives. He has betrayed the boys that were fortunate enough to return home. He has betrayed the Royal Canadian Legion, the daughters of the empire, many women's institutes, municipal councils, municipalities and thousands upon thousands of Canadians who have spent their money and their time making representations for the retention of the red ensign as Canada's national flag.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the just manner in which to deal with such an important issue is by referendum; let the Canadian people decide this issue. If such a vote were carried out,
I am certain that all parties would be united in carrying out the verdict of the electorate.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that time is running out. One is reminded of the fact that whom the gods would destroy they first make mad. This situation stems from the selfish lobby for control under which liberty becomes licensed and responsibility is replaced by self-consciousness; the welfare of the greatest number is prostituted to the pressures of the few. In this direction lies madness and death. This is not the way of democracy in which the few sacrificed self for the welfare of the many, when the spirit of sacrifice gives birth to liberty, freedom and trust, out of which grows the greatest good for the greatest number. Mr. Speaker, during the few remaining minutes, I should like to make a few comments in support of this resolution, a support which reflects the attitude and conviction of the majority of Canadians about the adoption of a national distinctive flag.
I consider as a great privilege to support that resolution on behalf of my constituents.
I also believe that the majority of the Canadian people are eagerly waiting for a distinctive national flag which will not be con-
Canadian Flag
fused with any other flag throughout the world.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, we live historic moments which will certainly etch the future of our beautiful country; the adoption of a new distinctive flag will show all the people of the globe, and in no uncertain terms, the sound determination of the Canadian parliament to take all the necessary means so as to be recognized everywhere as a mature nation, united and capable of self-government, able to command respect and provide for the welfare of its people, regardless of their ethnic origin.
Much has been written since the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) introduced this resolution on June 15 last; comments ranging from one extreme to the other, appeared in the newspapers. Even though I was only able to ascertain part of the views held by the main Canadian journalists, I think most of them are in favour of the prompt passage of this resolution.
However, I am more interested in the opinion of the average citizen. It is easy to realize that almost everybody, the young and the old, are greatly interested in the resolution. I find that most people were certain the resolution would be passed with a minimum of discussions and the majority wonder why this discussion must drag on for so long. I am happy to note that the younger generation especially, in every social class, is more interested in this resolution than in any other legislation now before the house. It is the most discussed subject among young people.
As a matter of fact, here is what a 12-year old boy told me in substance: When this resolution was introduced, I looked right away into my encyclopaedia to find out what emblem represented Canada; I saw the red ensign but that emblem is not a distinctive flag.
I feel that the interest shown by the people is a clear indication of the deep attachment each Canadian feels for his country; they show in their remarks that Canada is no longer, and has not been for a long time, a colony but is instead a free and autonomous country. For those reasons, the people favour the adoption of emblems which are typically Canadian and cannot be identified with those of any other country.
In my opinion, we have maintained long enough certain colonial ties which are humiliating for all those who believe in our country's maturity and independence; it is humiliating to be identified throughout the world by an emblem which is nothing but

a replica of the British merchant navy's; it is humiliating to be obliged to go to the British government to amend our own constitution; it is humiliating for all Canadians who have faith in Canada to see the word "British" so often linked with the word "Canadian"; it is humiliating to be identified still as just a part of the British empire; it is humiliating not to be now just plain Canadian citizens.
Many seem to promote the retention of the red ensign because large numbers of Canadians fought gloriously under that flag during two world wars. Yet, if you question some of those gallant citizens who risked everything on the front, it is obvious that the red ensign meant nothing to them and that most regiments had to fight under the union jack, the flag of another country.
Our courageous soldiers did not risk or sacrifice their lives for a symbol but to put an end to the unscrupulous domination by a people who were considered by their leader as superior to all other men, a racial superiority which does not exist in Canada more than anywhere else. It was mostly for the cause of freedom that Canadians accepted to fight and die in large numbers on the battlefields of Europe.

speechtext:
As one hon. member has just said, that depends on when the next election comes. But in any event, Mr. Speaker, it would add a very substantial number of voters. It is interesting to try and trace back to the origin of the idea that 21 years of age is the magic age at which young people pass from adolescence into adulthood. My analysis shows that this is a medieval belief. The idea of 21 years of age as the magic age for adulthood d/ates back to medieval times; it dates back to the days when the serfs were allowed to farm their own land at the age of 21. From that time stems the custom that has been perpetuated down through the centuries. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, it is time to get rid of some of these medieval customs that we perpetuate and bring them up to date and in line with the twentieth century.
I think it is a truism to assert that young people today 18 years of age are far better equipped to take part in public life than were the medieval serfs of centuries ago. Our young people today grow up in an entirely different environment. Attendance at school is now compulsory, and although our school curricula are very lacking in training in political and public matters, there are courses which equip our young people to take part in public life. Travel today is very swift and simple. Radio, television, newspapers and all the methods of communication and dissemination of news are very widely used on our young people are constantly exposed to current events and things that are taking place in the community. Therefore I think the 18 year old of today is far more knowledgeable than was his medieval ancestor and certainly ought to have the right to participate in voting for a particular government.

At 18 years of age, of course, one can marry without consent and can have children. At 16 years of age one may drive an automobile, which is potentially an instrument of death. If our young people 18 years of age are married and earn high enough incomes, we grant them the privilege of paying income tax, along with all the other people of this country, and their children receive the benefit of many welfare measures over which they have no control. I think the real basis of our concept of democratic government is that the greatest possible number of people who are going to be governed ought to participate in the method of choosing that government, as long as they are able to do so intelligently. I think this might encourage earlier voting habits, and perhaps these voting habits would be carried over into their later years.
This is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker. In making this change we timid Canadians need not really be worried that we are doing anything terribly radical or anything terribly different. In our own country, of course, we have examples of the voting age having been lowered. In the province of Quebec the 18 year old can vote, and this is also the case in Saskatchewan. British Columbia and Alberta both have the vote at 19 years of age. I happened to get in touch, with the help of our Canadian officials, with the United Nations and obtained an analysis of the countries in the United Nations which have already brought into effect legislation granting the vote to persons 18 years of age. There are some 32 countries in which the 18 year old can vote. So, as I say, Canadians would not be doing anything very spectacular, anything very different or anything very radical, in accepting this proposal.
The house might be interested to have these countries on the record. The following countries have the 18 year old vote: Albania, Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Bulgaria, Byelorussia, Burma, Ceylon, mainland China, Costa Rica, Czechoslovakia, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Indonesia, Israel, Mexico, the Mongolian People's Republic, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Paraguay, Poland, Rumania, Salvador, South Africa, Ukraine, Uraguay; Georgia, Kentucky and Alaska in the United States; the U.S.S.R., Venezuela, Yugoslavia, the Central African Republic, Congo, Brazzaville; Hungary, Iraq, the Ivory Coast, Laos, Ruanda, Somalia, Syria and South Viet Nam. Therefore, as I say, this practice has spread very widely in the world and it seems to me that a highly
Canada Elections Act
educated country like Canada ought to be prepared to adopt it. It is interesting, also, that in the United States a presidential commission appointed by the late President Kennedy has recommended that the 18 year old vote be put into effect in that country. This would add 9 million young Americans to the voting lists.
I should now like to deal with some of the arguments that are advanced against this proposal. The first is that the young people themselves do not want the 18 year old vote. One cannot find any evidence in support of this proposition; in fact, the evidence is all to the contrary. In a very interesting report prepared by an eminent member of the press gallery, Norman DePoe, and published in Weekend Magazine of April 11, 1964, this matter was dealt with. He reports on a survey conducted by Canadian High News, a paper with a circulation of 120,000 in our secondary schools, in which our students were asked the question as to whether the 18 year old should be given the vote. Sixty nine per cent voted in favour of this proposal. Several television programs have dealt with this matter. The C.B.C. program "Inquiry" conducted a survey and obtained roughly the same percentage in favour of it. So it is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that these young people do want to have the vote and do want to participate in the choosing of governments and approving or disapproving of government policies.
It is also sometimes suggested that these young people are not adequately prepared for and are not ready to have the vote. It is argued that their level of judgment and their knowledge of public affairs is not as high as that of their superiors, their parents, and that therefore they should be deprived of this vote. But the Canadian peace research institute, in trying to evaluate the importance of this matter and obtain the opinion of all sections of the population, conducted a very carefully prepared and precise investigation. They put a series of what they called knowledge questions to a section of the population from 18 years old, up. After it had been analysed and interpreted the report said that there were no significant differences between the teenage and adult samples on the eight knowledge questions. So that any precise examination that has been made of this young age group indicates that they are as adequately trained and prepared as the older groups.
I do not want to go into this at any great length because I think it is clear that

Canada Elections Act
throughout the history of voting every time the right to vote has been extended to another group in the community it has strengthened and improved popular government. It is also clear that the young people of today have every right to vote, that they are capable of voting, that they want to vote and that they would make a valuable contribution to the general good of our democratic system.
For the benefit of my Liberal friends the survey to which I referred showed that 93 per cent of our young people are in favour of "O Canada" as our national anthem. If hon. members opposite want to add a very large group of ardent supporters to their cause they had better bring in the 18 year old vote as quickly as possible.
I will not go any further into this point. As I said at the beginning this is a measure which has been unanimously supported by all parties in the house, and therefore it would be my hope that we would not talk this measure out or refer it back to the committee which has already approved it. I hope we might be able to pass it tonight and to make these young people eligible to vote at the general election everyone talks about as coming this fall.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE AGE OF VOTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few remarks to those of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott). I should like to align myself with his remarks. I am in favour of lowering the voting age to 18 years. As the hon. member stated, on Thursday, November 14 of last year, the standing committee on privileges and elections unanimously endorsed an amendment to section 14 of the Canada Elections Act to reduce the voting age from 21 to 18 years. Therefore, the 18, 19 and 20 year olds would be included and this would introduce some 750,000 to 800,000 new electors to the voting roll.
It may be fairly predicted that before long Canadians between 18 and 21 years of age will have the right to vote both in provincial and federal elections. This trend has already begun and its impetus is increasing. In the province of Saskatchewan the voting age is 18, in Alberta it is 19, in British Columbia 19, in Quebec it is 18 and in Newfoundland it is 19. In Manitoba it is interesting to note that the majority opinion of civic and provincial government officials supports 18 years of age as the voting age. The Winnipeg city council by a majority vote decided to ask the provincial government to change its city charter so that 18 year olds could vote in civic elec-

tions. Premier Robarts of Ontario has indicated that he will take similar action and give the franchise to 18 year olds in Ontario in time for the next provincial election.
In the province of Prince Edward Island the government has given an undertaking to amend the voting age in the province to conform with any change which is made in federal legislation.
As the hon. member for Danforth said, a move is afoot to lower the voting age in the United States for federal elections to 18 years of age. The President's commission on registration and voting participation which was set up by the late President Kennedy recommended to President Johnson on December 20, 1963 that all states consider dropping the minimum age for voters to 18 for state and federal elections.
Some people argue that the proposed step would mean the ruination of Canada. They say that the 18 year olds are not mature enough politically or otherwise to cast an intelligent vote. I think differently. The case for giving 18, 19 and 20 year olds the vote is realistic, sound and can stand on its own merits.
What are some of the arguments against lowering the voting age? First of all, it is said that an 18 year old's judgment is not as good on the average as it is at 21. I think this can be contradicted on many grounds. Second, it is said that the old-enough-to-fight argument is emotional because military standards are based on physical fitness and ability to learn, not on political awareness. Third, it is said that young drivers are more irresponsible; but some of the adults I have seen driving are more irresponsible than any person I have seen between the age of 18 and 21. Fourth, it is argued that the public should not be taken in by the aging platitudes of the political opportunists. Fifth, it is argued that under 21 years of age voters would not know what they were voting for, or would vote as society expects them to vote. I submit that this is a ridiculous argument.
It is interesting to note that the young Progressive Conservatives and the Progressive Conservative student federation voted against lowering the voting age. It is also interesting to observe that at the time the vote was taken at the meeting of February of this year there were not too many present, so perhaps that is one of the reasons for the vote. Many of the young Progressive Conservatives in my riding to whom I have spoken were in favour of lowering the voting

age. It is also interesting to note that in a statement which I read Mrs. J. J. Henderson, the secretary of the Winnipeg South Centre Progressive Conservative women's association, stated in a resolution which was passed that "Young people are not fully informed and don't give enough thought to politics". That is another argument against.
Then it is argued that few of them pay taxes or own property, which is another argument against lowering the age, because it is said that they would not use their ballots with the sober responsibility of someone with a stake in the community. Another reason against is because the vast majority could not care less about government and political affairs. I disagree with this. The last argument which is made is that the new electors may be pulled in a radical direction, and there is good reason to believe that by and large this would be disproved.
Nevertheless the arguments in favour of the extension of the voting age to 18 remain strong. The advantage of reducing the voting age is manifest. For example, it would directly involve these young people in the country's affairs. Given a direct voice in their country's destiny at an earlier age they could be expected to take an even greater interest in the nation's life than they do now, which would be all to the good for it would mean an extension of the democratic process.
I should like to give a short quotation from the Toronto Star for February 20, 1964, which reads as follows:
There is every reason to encourage young people to accept this basic obligation of citizenship at a time when its importance might be impressed upon them as part of their education.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that hundreds of thousands of young people finish high school at . 18 and begin to earn their own living. At 18 they come into the armed forces. At 18 many of them participate actively in politics and political parties. Political clubs at universities are now flourishing as seldom before. In fact when I attended university not too long ago it was unknown to have a political club of any party. Today there are many active political clubs at universities, and there are many mock parliaments not only at universities but in our high schools.
An 18 year old today is probably better informed and more interested in government affairs than are some of the parents of today. Today's higher standard of education has seen to that. The proportion of people with a high school education has greatly increased. Enrolment at universities of young people be-
Canada Elections Act
tween 18 and 21 years of age is growing each year. Less formal education, such as television and radio, is also bringing about a much earlier maturity. Improved educational facilities and wider experience are very good reasons for lowering the voting age. In maturing earlier, young people are taking an earlier interest in the political life of Canada, a political interest which must not be allowed to dissipate.
It must be captured, in the hope that it will be retained for life. Cited as the major argument for 18 year old voting by the United States presidential commission was the belief that by the time young people reach 21, they are-and I quote-"so removed from the stimulation of the educational process that their interest in public affairs has moved." It is in the late teens that an enthusiasm for political affairs often manifests itself; it is important for Canada that this be developed into constructive channels.
The right to vote is a valuable asset. It may help to crystallize an interest, to confer a sense of responsibility, and to give a better appreciation of the significance of the political process. Lowering the voting age is unlikely to bring any harm to the country. It would, rather, be taking advantage of assets of interest and enthusiasm which should have a helpful influence on Canadian political life. Whatever might have been true a few decades ago, today the great majority of young people have a degree of responsibility and of knowledge which would have been unknown to their parents until much later in their lives. A young person would be more inclined to turn out at the polls than his parents in response to the honour and responsibility he or she would feel on being given the franchise; he would probably shame his parents into going out to vote, too, since many of them now neglect to exercise their franchise.
With modern standards of education, most 18 year olds are much better prepared to vote than most of their grandparents were at 21 years of age. Andrew Robertson, chairman of the Winnipeg school board says-and I quote: "I have read some political essays written by high-schoolers and they show a better appraisal and understanding of government issues than their apathetic elders do." There is no reason to believe that Canada's young people are not mentally and emotionally equipped to vote at 18. It is significant that anyone serving in the armed forces, whether at home or abroad, is now entitled to vote in a federal election regardless of age

Canada Elections Act
and that he retains his voting rights on discharge even though he is still under 21.
A great many people in this country and elsewhere believed that the world would go up in smoke if women were ever given the right to vote. That is what they thought, but of course the world is still going on. If young Canadians were given the right and privilege of voting in national elections they would see it as an opportunity and as a challenge. And if they take, as they are now taking, an active part in politics they can make a substantial contribution to the Canadian democratic process. Canada is a nation of young people. Half the population is under 25 years of age and an estimated 67 per cent are younger than 40. In national elections young people can bring to bear a more objective, more detached and less self-interested judgment on party politics. Adoption of the lower voting age would recognize the increasing interest now being shown by Canada's young people in political activities. Participation by the younger generation in political affairs is symbolized in the makeup of this present parliament. The average age of members is somewhat lower today than the average age only ten years ago.
We should encourage our young people to take an earlier interest in public affairs for they will be the people responsible in the decades ahead for the maintenance and operation of our democratic institutions. As I stated earlier, the case for giving 18, 19 and 20 year olds the vote is realistic and sound and can stands on its own merits.
It is interesting to note that a move in this direction will not affect the course of the ship of state, since the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia and the others I mentioned earlier are still on solid foundations. It has not resulted in any dire consequences and I submit we should be realistic about the situation in which our young people find themselves. We give them every right except the right to exercise their franchise. The argument is often brought forward that legal responsibility is not recognized under the age of 21. I happen to be one of those who believe that legal responsibility might well be applied to young people at the age of 18, too, because more and more of these people are taking on commitments and increasingly it appears to me they should be legally responsible for them. However that may be, I endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Scott). I wish to support the lowering of the voting age from 21 to 18 and to [Mr. Macaluso.l
recommend to this house that it should either pass the bill or refer it to the standing committee on privileges and elections for reconsideration, since it has already unanimously approved an amendment to section 14 of the Canada Elections Act. Perhaps it might be wise to wait until that report comes forward, but I sincerely hope the house will support the stand being put forward this afternoon, because all parties represented on the committee supported the reduction of the age as recommended.

I cannot quarrel in any way with the statements made by the two previous speakers in setting forth reasons why the voting age should be reduced to 18. All those reasons are valid. Furthermore, there is very little which can be said against reducing the voting age I cannot put forward an argument which has often been used in the past, because I think for example that a person who is 18 may be just as able to cast an intelligent vote as a person who is over 21. I agree with these views, yet I am not convinced we should reduce the voting age.
If this bill had been brought in a year ago I would have supported it because I could see no reason to object to it. But there are some basic questions which have been brought up today and which I think we should consider. I think one of the most important was summarized in a statement made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) when he said: It can do no harm. I think these were the words he used. Over the years, the right to vote, particularly in a national election, has been very jealously guarded. In the early days, going back even to Roman times, the right to vote was severely restricted. Down through the years it has been extended and on occasions this extension has come about because a group of people who wanted to vote went out and worked for it. We know that in the early days lack of social or economic status was a barrier to the right to vote. People in a state of slavery or servitude were, of course, never allowed to vote. Eventually such people were released and all adult males were permitted to vote. Much later, as has already been mentioned, the women's vote was brought in. We can all remember the history of the great battle which went on for the right of women to vote in the United Kingdom and in Canada. This was a right which was fought for and won, and rightly so. This was the second great move forward in this field.

I assume the hon. member for Danforth in bringing forward this bill has evidence that the time is ripe for the third stage in the extension of the franchise, that is, the stage of reducing the voting age. But the difficulty that I see, and I have tested this to the best of my ability, is that the young people do not really want the vote.

I do not know how many were there or how many voted, but I do know that the recorded vote was 21 against and 6 in favour. I know that many did not vote on the resolution and that on another occasion to which I am coming the same thing happened. A large number of the young people did not vote because they said they did not care, that it meant nothing to them at all.
Before this rather shattering experience I thought I and my colleagues were really doing something for the young people of this country in supporting their request for the vote, but then I really got a shock when I found that they did not want it. Then I started to think about when 1 had ever heard of a request from a young people's group to reduce the voting age to 18 and I could not recall that there ever had been such a request.
Canada Elections Act
However, Mr. Speaker, since this matter had been raised and discussed in the committee on privileges and elections I decided that I had better find out what the young people of my own riding thought. So I conducted a series of discussion groups. One was at the Parry Sound high school. I was asked to come and discuss the matter because the students there had indicated some interest in it. It was a perfectly voluntary arrangement. There was a substantial turn-out of the students and as best I could I put to them the arguments for and the arguments against which we hear in this house and elsewhere. I asked them to consider this matter and let me know.
There were about 75 students present at that meeting. Eighteen voted in favour of reducing the voting age, 17 voted against and the remainder would not vote. They said they were not sufficiently acquainted with the political situation or politics or national affairs even to express an opinion whether or not they should vote. We all know that there are young people who are really interested in national affairs to the extent of working for political parties, but on the average young people do not take that much interest.
I also asked some of these young people whether they would be more interested in national affairs if they were given the vote. In other words, would this be an inducement to them to find out who was running, what the issues were and so forth? Some of them said they thought it might be but the majority said that while they might have some interest they were more interested in passing their examinations. This was the attitude revealed in the answers I received.
We in this house seem to be doing a lot of thinking these days about what the people want. We are in the midst of a flag debate and many of us are trying to find out what our constituents really think and want. The same is true of the voting age problem. We would really like to know what our own constituents think, what the public think and particularly what the young people think. But I say we do not know. There has been no evidence one way or the other. I say also that until we do know we should not change. Change is only beneficial when it is for the better and until it is proven that change will be beneficial we should not change at all.
With this in mind I do not believe that the time has come to reduce the voting age in Canada. As I say, I am naturally in favour of reducing the voting age for young people if they want the vote. But I do not think it

Canada Elections Act
is good enough for us to say that it will not do any harm, that they will vote the same way as their parents and so forth. This is not a good enough reason to extend the franchise to another large group of voters.
I do not think anyone will argue against the fact that as you grow older you grow a little wiser. I think that at age 21 people have probably learned a little more about life than at age 18. I believe there is a definable difference between people at age 18 and at age 21, and I think we must recognize it. Until we can be shown that there is a great desire on the part of these young people to reduce the voting age I do not think we should do it.
This was not the only group to which I spoke. I spoke to several others and the results were about the same. In other words, some were for, some were against and just as many either did not care or would not express an opinion. This is not an indication of a great desire on the part of young people between 18 and 20 to have the vote in national elections. I think the right to vote is a right that must be fought for and won. It is not something we should give without being asked to do so.
I appreciate the fact that the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) has brought this matter forward in the hope that we may perhaps run a little bit ahead of the feeling of the young people and give the vote to them before they want it, but in any aspect of life I do not think people appreciate anything given freely which they do not really want. For that reason I think we should move very slowly on this matter.
There is another problem which concerns the standing committee on privileges and elections. Technically I think there is nothing before that committee now because their proceedings came to an end when the last session finished, and their report was not adopted. I do not happen to be a member of that committee but I did read the evidence because I wanted to find out what had been said in the standing committee on privileges and elections which influenced the members to support such a move.
I found this subject had been introduced into this committee suddenly, and without notice, by a combination of a Liberal member and an N.D.P. member. The question was put and members found themselves on the spot. Members who were there apparently decided, well, we would be better off to vote for it than against it because if we vote against it we will be in an impossible position; but if we vote for it at least we will vote

for something that will do no serious harm. I still go along with this view. It will not do any harm. There will not be any great catastrophe if we reduce the voting age. I merely say it is not going to do any great amount of good. It is not being requested by the young people and therefore the move has not reached the stage when it should be accepted.
The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) who introduced this bill said he could not find any evidence to support the proposition that young people did not want it. I agree with him on that. I do not think there is any evidence. Any evidence I can gather indicates they are indifferent to the whole problem. I can say, Mr. Speaker, that if I were not fairly sure of my ground I would not be standing here and saying so. If I felt that young people really wanted the right to vote, that they really ought to have it, then I would be prepared to support this measure. I do not feel that way. I feel that if they did get it, those who would go to vote would do the best they could. I do not see any great harm arising. However I am not at all hesitant about standing in my place today and saying that the time has not yet come for a reduction in the voting age to 18 for national elections.
The hon. member for Danforth mentioned a large number of states which had reduced the voting age for national elections. Most of these states or countries were what I might call socialist states. This might not be the proper term, but except for three of the states of the United States, none of those states mentioned by the hon. member was what I would call a state of the western world-except perhaps Israel and one or two others. I was particularly looking for countries like the United States, Australia, New Zealand, France, Britain and the Netherlands. None of those countries has reduced the voting age to 18. I am not too much impressed by the list the hon. member read.
I will admit that in the state of Israel they are making great progress in bringing about social reform. They are making great effort to bring their young people into the national light. I think this is a good thing. They have, perhaps different circumstances than we have. With this one exception, and perhaps one or two others, I do not accept the list of nations which have reduced their national voting age as being impressive to the point of persuading us in Canada to reduce our voting age.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that is the sum total of my remarks. We are having a full consideration of the elections act by the standing committee on privileges and elections. I believe seldom, if ever, has it been the custom that while a committee is considering a certain matter, has gone through the motions at least of considering the whole of the elections act, that we in this house should introduce a bill anticipating the recommendations of that committee. It may be said that there was unanimous agreement in the committee, but when the report of the committee is introduced I am sure there will be considerable debate on many of the amendments proposed to the Canada Elections Act. For that reason, I do not believe this is the proper time to introduce this measure. In this respect, I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso). I took it that he was somewhat doubtful as to whether or not this was the proper procedure, to introduce this bill at this time. I agree with him. However, I am not going to hide behind that. I do not think it is time to reduce the voting age to 18.

It has been pointed out that they serve in the armed forces. They occupy positions of some prominence and responsibility in various fields and, therefore, should have the opportunity of casting their ballots and making
Canada Elections Act
their choice of a representative. We feel, therefore, it is a principle of democracy that, so far as possible, those who are subject to government should have a choice of the organ that governs them. We talk about the fact that democracy is government with the consent of the governed. It seems therefore, Mr. Speaker, that they should have an opportunity to indicate their willingness to be governed by a certain representative, and this would be in the interests of all concerned. We feel, again, it would encourage young people to take an interest in politics at an age when they are still in school. Therefore they would give themselves to a study of the respective platforms of political parties. They would seek to understand various political philosophies and inform themselves as to the issues confronting the country. If this could be done it would be a very worth-while accomplishment.
Young people just standing on the threshold of life have more at stake in the future than those who are older in age. If they are able to stand the stress of life they will live longer, and therefore will be longer affected by the activities and decisions of government. A lot of young people are taxpayers, many of them possibly at the age of 18 years. At a time when so much of the government's revenue is taken from ordinary taxpayers to meet the expenses of government, surely as many taxpayers as possible should have the opportunity of expressing their opinions with respect to those who will be legislating for them and imposing taxes upon them.
It has been suggested that young people are not qualified to express intelligently their views on matters of government. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, there are a great many young people aged 18 and 19-I am not going to be a sticker for either age, although I think possibly 19 might be better-who are more qualified than older people of a far greater age. Young people take a keen interest and are not afraid to make decisions while many older people tend to settle down and say, "So long as I can make a living I can get along. Leave it to the young people."
I do not intend to take up the remaining time as there may be other members who wish to speak on this measure, and I certainly do not want to talk it out. Reference has been made to the article written by Norman DePoe in Weekend Magazine of March, 1964. On page 3 of that article we find:
The students union council of the University of Manitoba.. .passed a vote supporting retention of the voting age at 21.

Yes, I am aware that if I speak now I will kill this and, yes, that is exactly my intention, because I do not think for one moment that now is an opportune time in this country's affairs to lower the voting age to 18.
I may say I am quite aware of the very intelligent interest shown by many of that age, and I have had the benefit of their hard work in my own election campaigns. I may say they are just as serious as the 21 year elds; sometimes they are much harder working, but I think this is only a very small percentage of them. They make a very impressive mark; but the point I have made in this house previously on this subject is that voting is not just a case of intelligence and hard work.
Voting requires judgment, and judgment in this day and age requires an ever increasing amount of education to begin to comprehend the problems the country faces. It cannot be achieved while one is still encompassed with that very harsh problem of trying to catch up to this modern age. I say judgment is the result of education, intelligence and experience. Today if any change in the voting age is required, in keeping with conditions in the country, in keeping with the requirements of our modern technological society it would, if anything, be to raise the voting age.
A few years ago when comparatively little education was required a man could cope with life at 15 if he were full grown and had his full strength, but now it takes more and more education and experience and now, more than ever, if we are to run this country properly, if we are to have votes cast properly, there must be judgment. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in saying I hope this will go no further at this time. May I call it six o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE AGE OF VOTERS
speechtext:
The hour
for consideration of private members' business has expired.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would like to ask the acting house leader about the business for next week?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
On Monday we will resume the committee stage of Bill C-90, an act to amend the National Defence Act. When the committee and third reading stage are concluded we will consider second reading stage of the bill relating to youth allowances. We will then take up the committee stage
Business of the House of Bill S-17, respecting the territorial sea and fishing zones of Canada. This bill has been considered by the standing committee on marine and fisheries and referred back to the house.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.
Monday, July 6, 1964
